author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — accessibility: Code header areas in the accordion as buttons.
statement: Code header areas in the accordion as buttons. Using a assures accordions are usable with both screen readers and keyboards.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — accessibility: Use meaningful expansion button labels.
statement: Use meaningful expansion button labels. Aim for informative labels like “Explore federal compliance checklists” rather than vague ones like “Click here.”

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — accessibility: Use aria-controls to associate an accordion button with its related content.
statement: Use aria-controls to associate an accordion button with its related content. Connect an accordion button control with its appropriate content region by referencing the controlled element’s id in the button's aria-controls attribute.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — accessibility: Use unique ids.
statement: Use unique ids. Each button has a unique name, aria-controls="[id]", that associates the control with the appropriate region by referencing the controlled element’s id.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — accessibility: Accordions use javascript to set the hidden values of their content areas.
statement: Accordions use javascript to set the hidden values of their content areas. Each content area will have its hidden attribute set by the component, depending on its corresponding button’s aria-expanded attribute. To ensure your content is accessible in the event that the JavaScript does not load or is disabled, you should not manually set hidden on any of your content areas.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — accessibility: You do not need to add text alternatives for the collapsed and expanded accordion states.
statement: You do not need to add text alternatives for the collapsed and expanded accordion states. These states are set programmatically with JavaScript.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — implementation: Multiselectable accordion groups.
statement: Multiselectable accordion groups. Add the data-allow-multiple attribute to any usa-accordion to create a multiselectable accordion group.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — implementation: Default an accordion button to open.
statement: Default an accordion button to open. Add the aria-expanded="true" attribute to any usa-accordionbutton to have that section open by default at page load. When the accordion is initialized, the JavaScript will automatically add aria-expanded="false" attribute to all other accordion buttons.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — implementation: Accordion icon position.
statement: Accordion icon position. The expand/collapse icon defaults to the start side of the accordion. “Start” refers to the reading order of the language — this means for languages that are read left to right (English, Spanish, etc.), the expand/collapse icon will default to the left. For languages that are read right to left (Arabic, Hebrew, etc.), the expand/collapse icon will default to the right. Previous to USWDS 3.14.0, the icon defaulted to the end side.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — implementation: Set icon position.
statement: Set icon position. To change accordion icon placement everywhere an accordion appears, use the $theme-accordion-icon-position setting ("start" or "end"). To change icon placement for a single accordion, add usa-accordion--icon-start or usa-accordion--icon-end to the accordion root.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — usability: Make the entire header selectable.
statement: Make the entire header selectable. Allow users to click anywhere in the header area to expand or collapse the content; a larger target is easier to manipulate.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — usability: Give interactive elements enough space.
statement: Give interactive elements enough space. Make sure interactive elements within the collapsible region are far enough from the headers that users don’t accidentally trigger a collapse. (The exact distance depends on the device.)

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Accordion — when to consider something else
title: Accordion — when to consider something else: If users need to see most or all of the information on a page.
statement: If users need to see most or all of the information on a page. Use well-formatted text instead.
citation: USWDS. Accordion — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Accordion — when to consider something else
title: Accordion — when to consider something else: If there is not enough content to warrant condensing.
statement: If there is not enough content to warrant condensing. Accordions increase cognitive load and interaction cost because users have to make decisions about what headers to click on.
citation: USWDS. Accordion — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Accordion — when to use: If users will only need a few specific pieces of content within a page.
statement: If users will only need a few specific pieces of content within a page. - If you have only a small space to display a lot of content.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — accessibility: Start the alert’s text with a word describing the alert type.
statement: Start the alert’s text with a word describing the alert type. Specify the type of alert in the first word of its text. Depending on the type of alert component (informative, warning, etc.), that text may be set as heading or body copy. Users should be able to understand the purpose of the alert without relying solely on its color or the shape of its icon. If leading with the alert type makes the alert itself unclear, consider including it in the body text.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — accessibility: Use the appropriate alert type.
statement: Use the appropriate alert type. - Informative: Non-critical information, such as status. For informative alert types, consider using “Announcement” or a more precise term as the first word.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — accessibility: Warning:
statement: Warning: Potentially critical information that might impact the experience or require action.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — accessibility: Success:
statement: Success: Information that indicates an action was successful.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — accessibility: Error:
statement: Error: Information that indicates an action failed.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — accessibility: Emergency:
statement: Emergency: Critical, high-priority information that will impact the experience and might require immediate action.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — accessibility: Don’t visually hide alert messages and then make them visible when they are needed.
statement: Don’t visually hide alert messages and then make them visible when they are needed. Users of older assistive technologies may still be able to perceive the alert messages even if they are not currently applicable.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — accessibility: Use the proper ARIA role.
statement: Use the proper ARIA role. The ARIA role attribute can notify assistive technologies of time-sensitive and important messages. To elevate the importance of the alert, choose the appropriate role from the ARIA roles table and add it to the .usa-alert element.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — usability: Create short and clear alert titles.
statement: Create short and clear alert titles. The alert heading should include the alert type and can provide more about the alert, but shouldn’t include more than one line of text. Add any additional alert details in the body text of the alert.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — usability: Consider next steps.
statement: Consider next steps. When the user is required to do something in response to an alert, let them know what they need to do, and make that task as easy as possible. Think about how much context to provide with your message. For example, a system status message may require more contextual information than a validation message. Write the message in concise, human-readable language; avoid jargon and computer code.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — usability: Be polite.
statement: Be polite. Be polite in error messages — don’t blame the user.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — usability: Alerts are an opportunity.
statement: Alerts are an opportunity. Users will read a message that helps them resolve an error even if they generally won’t read documentation; include some educational material in your error message.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — usability: Don’t overdo it.
statement: Don’t overdo it. Too many notifications will either overwhelm or annoy the user and are likely to be ignored.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — usability: Allow a user to dismiss a notification whenever appropriate.
statement: Allow a user to dismiss a notification whenever appropriate. USWDS is working on a way to help developers implement a dismissible alert. You can follow our progress on GitHub.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — usability: Understand the user’s context.
statement: Understand the user’s context. Don’t include notifications that aren’t related to the user’s current goal.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Alert — when to consider something else
title: Alert — when to consider something else: Long forms.
statement: Long forms. On long forms, always include in-line validation in addition to any error messages that appear at the top of the form.
citation: USWDS. Alert — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Alert — when to consider something else
title: Alert — when to consider something else: Destructive actions.
statement: Destructive actions. If an action will result in destroying a user’s work (for example, deleting an application) use a more intrusive pattern, such as a confirmation modal dialogue, to allow the user to confirm that this action is what they want.
citation: USWDS. Alert — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — when to use: System status messages.
statement: System status messages. An alert may be a notification that keeps people informed of the status of the system and may or may not require the user to respond. Such notifications may be errors, warnings, and general updates.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Alert — when to use: Validation messages.
statement: Validation messages. An alert may be a validation message that informs a user they just took an action that needs to be corrected or a confirmation that a task was completed successfully.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — accessibility: Use the nav element.
statement: Use the nav element. This allows assistive technology to present the breadcrumbs in context as a navigational element on the page.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — accessibility: Treat separators as text when it comes to contrast.
statement: Treat separators as text when it comes to contrast. Use separators that have AA contrast against their background.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — accessibility: Use ordered lists and list items.
statement: Use ordered lists and list items. Use an ol for breadcrumbs and an li for each item. This allows assistive technology to enumerate the items in the breadcrumbs and allows shortcuts between list items.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — accessibility: Use ARIA markup for additional context.
statement: Use ARIA markup for additional context. Use aria-label="Breadcrumbs" on the main element and aria-current="page" on the current page.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — accessibility: Hide separators from screen readers.
statement: Hide separators from screen readers. The separators between links in the breadcrumbs should not be read by screen readers.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — usability: Consider alternatives to wrapping.
statement: Consider alternatives to wrapping. In general, rely on truncating the title of the current page over wrapping breadcrumb text. But usability comes first. Consider alternative approaches if the title of the current page is completely truncated. For example, a mobile-friendly breadcrumb may show only a page's direct parent. Sites with very long breadcrumb trails might ultimately need to wrap breadcrumbs, or consider flattening the information architecture of the site.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — usability: Use complete page titles.
statement: Use complete page titles. Use the same wording in breadcrumb text as in the page title.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — usability: Start with the word “Home”.
statement: Start with the word “Home”. Rather than using a house icon, spell out the word “Home” as the first link in the breadcrumbs.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — usability: Consider size of tap targets on small widths.
statement: Consider size of tap targets on small widths. Although breadcrumbs are frequently displayed using smaller text, make sure the text is not too small to select at small widths.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — usability: Optimize for search engines.
statement: Optimize for search engines. To be eligible for rich results display in search engine results, mark up your site’s breadcrumbs using JSON-LD (recommended) or RDFa.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Breadcrumb — when to consider something else
title: Breadcrumb — when to consider something else: Simple sites.
statement: Simple sites. If the website is not very deep and the context for the current page is clear from the main navigation.
citation: USWDS. Breadcrumb — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Breadcrumb — when to consider something else
title: Breadcrumb — when to consider something else: Landing pages.
statement: Landing pages. Omit breadcrumbs on the homepage of a site. Breadcrumbs could also be omitted from section landing pages. Breadcrumbs are most useful when the hierarchy is not immediately apparent from the main navigation.
citation: USWDS. Breadcrumb — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Breadcrumb — when to consider something else
title: Breadcrumb — when to consider something else: Redundant side navigation.
statement: Redundant side navigation. When side navigation is used in combination with main navigation, it may be redundant to include breadcrumbs.
citation: USWDS. Breadcrumb — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Breadcrumb — when to consider something else
title: Breadcrumb — when to consider something else: Step-by-step processes.
statement: Step-by-step processes. Use breadcrumbs for hierarchical relationships, not linear relationships (like individual steps in a multi-step process).
citation: USWDS. Breadcrumb — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — when to use: When orientation matters.
statement: When orientation matters. Breadcrumbs show where the current page is located in the website hierarchy. Use a breadcrumb when it's likely that a user will arrive at an interior page from search or from an outside link.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Breadcrumb — when to use: To facilitate navigation.
statement: To facilitate navigation. Breadcrumbs make it easier to understand complex sites. Use breadcrumbs to reinforce your site's structure.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — accessibility: Buttons should display a visible focus state when users tab to them.
statement: Buttons should display a visible focus state when users tab to them. - Use standard markup. Avoid using or tags to create buttons. Screen readers don't automatically know either is a usable button.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — accessibility: Screen readers handle buttons and links differently.
statement: Screen readers handle buttons and links differently. When styling links to look like buttons, remember that screen readers handle links slightly differently than they do buttons. Pressing the Space key triggers a button, but pressing the Enter key triggers a link.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — accessibility: Keep unavailable actions understandable.
statement: Keep unavailable actions understandable. Explain why an action is unavailable and how to make it available. A native disabled button is removed from the tab order. An aria-disabled="true" button stays in the tab order, but your application must prevent activation by mouse, keyboard, and other input methods.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — implementation: Always set the type attribute.
statement: Always set the type attribute. Define the purpose and behavior of a button with the type attribute. The type attribute can accept three values: submit, button, and reset. If no type attribute is defined, the button will behave as a submit button.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — implementation: Use the disabled or aria-disabled attributes to turn on disabled button styles.
statement: Use the disabled or aria-disabled attributes to turn on disabled button styles. - Add button styles to links. To use a button style on a link, add the usa-button class to your link. Add an additional button variant class to access variant styles.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — implementation: Disabled styles do not replace disabled behavior.
statement: Disabled styles do not replace disabled behavior. The native disabled attribute prevents activation of a . aria-disabled="true" communicates the state and applies USWDS styles, but does not prevent activation by itself. Add application logic to prevent the action. The disabled attribute does not disable an element.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — usability: Use standard buttons for actions that go a next step.
statement: Use standard buttons for actions that go a next step. - Use outline buttons for actions that happen on the current page.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — usability: Give an important action a distinctive style.
statement: Give an important action a distinctive style. Style the button most users should select in a way that distinguishes it from other buttons on the page. Try using the usa-button--big variant or the most visually distinct color variant.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — usability: Make sure buttons look selectable.
statement: Make sure buttons look selectable. Use color variations to distinguish static, hover, and active states.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — usability: Avoid using too many buttons on a page.
statement: Avoid using too many buttons on a page. - Use sentence-case capitalization for button labels.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — usability: Keep button text short.
statement: Keep button text short. Button text should be as short as possible with action words that clearly explain what will happen when the button is selected (for example, Download, View, or Sign up).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — usability: Lead with a verb.
statement: Lead with a verb. Make the first word of the button’s text a verb. For example, instead of Complaint filing, label the button File a complaint.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — usability: Icons can be helpful.
statement: Icons can be helpful. Consider adding an icon to signal specific actions (Download, Open in a new window, etc).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Button — when to consider something else
title: Button — when to consider something else: Linking between a site’s pages.
statement: Linking between a site’s pages. Use regular links instead.
citation: USWDS. Button — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Button — when to consider something else
title: Button — when to consider something else: If the action is less popular or less important.
statement: If the action is less popular or less important. Less popular or less important actions may be visually styled as links.
citation: USWDS. Button — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Button — when to use: Important actions.
statement: Important actions. Use buttons for the most important actions you want users to take on your site, such as Download, Sign up or Log out.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — accessibility: Use unordered lists and list items.
statement: Use unordered lists and list items. Use a ul for a card group and an li for each card. This formatting allows screen readers to enumerate the items in the card group and allows shortcuts between list items.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — accessibility: Use the appropriate heading level for your page.
statement: Use the appropriate heading level for your page. Update heading level based on the content of your page to make sure card headings are in the correct, logical outline order.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — accessibility: Use CSS to order the media element.
statement: Use CSS to order the media element. Logically, the media element should follow the header element. Don't re-organize the markup to reverse their order.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — implementation: Control card size and layout with USWDS utilities.
statement: Control card size and layout with USWDS utilities. The card component works well with layout grid utilities. The usa-card-group block is functionally a wrap-able grid-row, and each individual usa-card is a grid-col. This means you can use a grid utility like tablet:grid-col-4 to set a four-column size on a card at tablet width. You can also set custom grid gaps on a usa-card-group using grid-gap utilities.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — implementation: Control image aspect ratio with the add-aspect utility.
statement: Control image aspect ratio with the add-aspect utility. Add aspect ratio utility classes to usa-cardimg or usa-cardmedia elements to control the aspect ratio on card images. Alternatively, control aspect ratio in your Sass files via the add-aspect mixin.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — implementation: Style cards with utilities.
statement: Style cards with utilities. Style the usa-cardcontainer element with utilities to achieve custom effects, such as changing the border or background color or adding a drop shadow.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — usability: Make cards actionable.
statement: Make cards actionable. Since cards are used as a summary of more detailed information, any individual card should link out to that information.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — usability: Don't use the card component only for decoration.
statement: Don't use the card component only for decoration. Use the card component for cards, not for any type of content that's designed to have a border around it.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — usability: Include non-redundant content.
statement: Include non-redundant content. Don't repeat images or content common to all or most cards in a collection. Repeated information (like using the same image for each card in a collection) makes it more difficult to distinguish cards from one another.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — usability: Make sure images are properly sized.
statement: Make sure images are properly sized. Cards often change size depending on the device. Make sure you use an image that works well on any device at any size.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — usability: Use simple styling.
statement: Use simple styling. Avoid distracting skeumorphism. Don't include any card styling that calls too much attention to the metaphor of a paper card, like folds, bent edges, or paper texture.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Card — when to consider something else
title: Card — when to consider something else: Tabular data.
statement: Tabular data. Don't use a card as a substitute for a table row.
citation: USWDS. Card — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Card — when to consider something else
title: Card — when to consider something else: Simple calls to action.
statement: Simple calls to action. Use a button instead.
citation: USWDS. Card — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Card — when to consider something else
title: Card — when to consider something else: Standalone content.
statement: Standalone content. Consider an aside or another standalone element.
citation: USWDS. Card — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Card — when to consider something else
title: Card — when to consider something else: Sequential, continuous text.
statement: Sequential, continuous text. Cards should be self-contained and modular. If the reader is meant to read from card to card, consider a list or simple body text and headings.
citation: USWDS. Card — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Card — when to use: Collections of related content.
statement: Collections of related content. Cards help present a collection of related groups of content, like articles or sections of a website.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Character Count — accessibility: Associate the character count message to the input.
statement: Associate the character count message to the input. Use aria-describedby on the input to allow the message to be announced to those using screen readers.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Character Count — implementation: Add component classes.
statement: Add component classes. The structure should include a base element with the class usa-character-count. Inside of that base element there should be an input element (input or textarea) with the class usa-character-countfield and an message element (span or div) with the class usa-character-countmessage.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Character Count — implementation: Add a maxlength attribute to the input element.
statement: Add a maxlength attribute to the input element. This will be used as the limit referenced in the message and for validation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Character Count — implementation: Provide a backup message for environments without JavaScript.
statement: Provide a backup message for environments without JavaScript. In your markup, add a default message in the usa-character-countmessage element that refers to the character limit. This will appear in instances when JavaScript does not load.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Character Count — when to consider something else
title: Character Count — when to consider something else: Backend limitations.
statement: Backend limitations. If your users keep hitting the character limit imposed by the backend of your service then try to increase the limit rather than use a character count.
citation: USWDS. Character Count — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Character Count — when to consider something else
title: Character Count — when to consider something else: Already implied.
statement: Already implied. If the character length is apparent or implied by the data type (i.e. phone number or zip code).
citation: USWDS. Character Count — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Character Count — when to consider something else
title: Character Count — when to consider something else: Exceeding the character limit is highly unlikely.
statement: Exceeding the character limit is highly unlikely. If the vast majority of users (well over 99%) are very unlikely to run afoul of backend validation, such as an address field that has a database field limit of 250 characters.
citation: USWDS. Character Count — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Character Count — when to use: Brevity is desired.
statement: Brevity is desired. When users are likely to provide more detail than is needed, and you want to force them to use fewer words. Note: this will likely increase the amount of time it takes users to submit the form because editing requires thinking. In the words of Mark Twain, “I didn't have time to write a short letter, so I wrote a long one instead.”
citation: USWDS. Character Count — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Character Count — when to use: Legal requirement.
statement: Legal requirement. When there is a legal reason where an entry must be under a certain number of characters.
citation: USWDS. Character Count — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — accessibility: Use a fieldset and legend for a checkbox group.
statement: Use a fieldset and legend for a checkbox group. Surround a related set of checkboxes with a . The provides context for the grouping. Don’t use fieldset and legend for a single check.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — accessibility: These custom checkboxes are accessible.
statement: These custom checkboxes are accessible. The custom checkboxes here are accessible to screen readers because the default checkboxes are moved off-screen with position: absolute; left: -999em.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — accessibility: Use semantic tags.
statement: Use semantic tags. Each input should have a semantic tag for the id attribute, and its corresponding label should have the same value in its for attribute.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — usability: Make the label selectable.
statement: Make the label selectable. Users should be able to select either the text label or the checkbox to select or deselect an option.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — usability: List options vertically.
statement: List options vertically. Horizontal listings can make it difficult to tell which label pertains to which checkbox.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — usability: Use positive statements.
statement: Use positive statements. Negative language in labels can be counterintuitive. For example, use “I want to receive a promotional email” instead of “I don’t want to receive a promotional email.”

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — usability: Use logical labels.
statement: Use logical labels. Make sure that the label makes both states — checked and unchecked — clear to the user. If that’s not possible, consider using a radio button with two individual options instead. Then both states can have their own clearly marked label.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — usability: Use adequate touch targets.
statement: Use adequate touch targets. Make sure selections are adequately spaced for touch screens. Consider using the tile variant for larger touch targets.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — usability: Don’t mix default and tile variants.
statement: Don’t mix default and tile variants. Pick one implementation and stick with it. When mixed, tiles can appear to indicate a bias or preference toward that option.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — usability: Use a logical order.
statement: Use a logical order. Make sure the selection options are organized in a meaningful way, like alphabetical or most-frequent to least-frequent. This helps users easily find the option they’re looking for.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Checkbox — when to consider something else
title: Checkbox — when to consider something else: Single-select only.
statement: Single-select only. If a user can only select one option from a list of many, use radio buttons instead.
citation: USWDS. Checkbox — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — when to use: To display multiple answers.
statement: To display multiple answers. When a user can select any number of choices from a list.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Checkbox — when to use: To allow users to toggle answers.
statement: To allow users to toggle answers. When a user needs to acknowledge acceptance of something (like terms of service) or switch between two opposite states, such as unchecked = “no” and checked = “yes.”

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — accessibility: Use unordered lists and list items.
statement: Use unordered lists and list items. Use a ul for a collection and an li for each item. This allows screen readers to enumerate the items in the collection and allows shortcuts between list items.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — accessibility: Use the appropriate heading level for your page.
statement: Use the appropriate heading level for your page. Update heading levels based on the content of your page to make sure collection headings are in the correct logical outline order..

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — accessibility: Each link should have a unique name.
statement: Each link should have a unique name. Those using assistive technology may collect all page links together. Unique names not only help these users distinguish between links, but help all users scan the page. Favor using link text itself to provide a unique name. Using a title attribute or aria-label to provide a unique name helps users of assistive technology, but doesn't promote scannability in standard browsers.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — implementation: Collection — implementation
statement: - See the code samples on this page for examples of the content types available to a collection: - Heading - Description - Thumbnail image - Calendar date - Meta information

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — usability: Use thumbnail images consistently.
statement: Use thumbnail images consistently. If you use a thumbnail image on one item, use a similar kind of image (photo, illustration, etc.) on every item in the collection. Ensure icons or illustrations have clear meaning that add value or context to the content. Avoid repeating placeholder images.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — usability: Use a consistent width for images.
statement: Use a consistent width for images. Display item images with a consistent width. This promotes consistent alignment and easy scannability.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — usability: Avoid ambiguous, generic article links like “read more.”
statement: Avoid ambiguous, generic article links like “read more.” The heading for each item should link to the full content. Ensure each heading is clear, concise, and unique so users can quickly understand what the content is about. Don’t include additional links that take users to the same place.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — usability: Use a descriptive title.
statement: Use a descriptive title. The collection's title should make the collection's theme clear — for example, “Recent posts,” “How-to videos,” or “Resources about flu shots.”

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — usability: Link to additional related content, if applicable.
statement: Link to additional related content, if applicable. Collections may not include every piece of content related to its theme. If there's a location that collects more comprehensive results related to the theme, add a link to that location.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — usability: Provide a button or link to where more articles can be found.
statement: Provide a button or link to where more articles can be found. Users may need access to an index or archive where they can find more articles than those listed in the component.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — usability: Provide a strong "information scent" for each article.
statement: Provide a strong "information scent" for each article. Use headings, teaser text, a thumbnail image, and meta information effectively to help users understand the value of each item and choose which ones to visit.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — usability: Indicate to the user if they'll navigate to another website.
statement: Indicate to the user if they'll navigate to another website. A common way to do this is to add the external link class to the heading if the link takes you away from the current site.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — usability: Don’t force in-page scrolling.
statement: Don’t force in-page scrolling. Display all collection items in a flexible container so it displays without forcing the user to scroll within a component container. You can help prevent this by limiting the number of items in the collection to six or fewer.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Collection — when to consider something else
title: Collection — when to consider something else: Providing an archive of articles or pages.
statement: Providing an archive of articles or pages. Consider limiting the number of items in each collection to six or fewer. If you need to allow users to search or browse a larger content catalog, consider using a separate index or archive page.
citation: USWDS. Collection — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Collection — when to consider something else
title: Collection — when to consider something else: When you want to display large images or other media.
statement: When you want to display large images or other media. Collections are meant to be compact. If you need something with large images or other media, consider using the card component. The card has a bigger footprint and provides more flexibility with large images and other media.
citation: USWDS. Collection — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — when to use: To feature content with its metadata.
statement: To feature content with its metadata. The collection component is a good option when displaying content that should be accompanied by limited metadata like tags, date/time, or source and attribution.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — when to use: To group related content together.
statement: To group related content together. The collection component can provide links to articles from a trusted source, popular guides and resources, or a collection of pages that cover different aspects of a single topic.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Collection — when to use: To collect items from multiple sources.
statement: To collect items from multiple sources. Use collections when you want to guide users to additional resources available elsewhere. Collections introduce themes that help users find what they’re looking for, including when it's not on your site.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — accessibility: Known assistive technology issues.
statement: Known assistive technology issues. Testing with people using assistive technology revealed usability concerns that require additional investigation. At this time, consider using a Select component instead of a Combo box. More research and testing is planned to better understand and address these accessibility issues. If you would like to contribute to improving this component, please join our community and share your feedback.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — accessibility: Always use a label.
statement: Always use a label. Make sure your select element has a label. Don’t replace it with the default menu option (for example, removing the “State” label and just having the menu read “Select a state” by default).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — accessibility: Avoid auto-submission.
statement: Avoid auto-submission. Don’t use JavaScript to automatically submit the form (or do anything else) when an option is selected. Auto-submission disrupts screen readers because they select each option as they read them.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — implementation: Properties.
statement: Properties. The following properties modify component functionality. These properties can be set or adjusted at any time before or after initialization in order to have an effect.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — implementation: Initialization properties.
statement: Initialization properties. The following properties update the component during initialization. These properties must be set before the component is initialized in order to have an effect.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — implementation: Procedures.
statement: Procedures. The following static procedures update the component after initialization. These are in addition to the primary methods referenced in the JS customization documentation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — usability: Use option strings familiar to users.
statement: Use option strings familiar to users. The combo box filters by matching strings. Include option text that includes familiar strings or spellings (for example, if using the combobox with a state list, include the postal abbreviation in the option text: District of Columbia (DC)).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — usability: Make sure to test.
statement: Make sure to test. Test select menus thoroughly with members of your target audience. Several usability experts suggest they should be the “UI of last resort.” Many users find them confusing and difficult to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — usability: Avoid dependent options.
statement: Avoid dependent options. Avoid making options in one select menu change based on the input to another. Users often don’t understand how choosing an item in one impacts another

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — usability: Use a good default.
statement: Use a good default. When most users will (or should) pick a particular option, make it the default: Default .

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — usability: Avoid auto-submission.
statement: Avoid auto-submission. Don’t use JavaScript to automatically submit the form (or do anything else) when an option is selected. Offer a “submit” button at the end of the form instead. Users often change their choices multiple times. Auto-submission is also less accessible.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Combo Box — when to consider something else
title: Combo Box — when to consider something else: Limited choices.
statement: Limited choices. When the number of options is small, you can continue to use a select or radio element.
citation: USWDS. Combo Box — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — when to use: More than 15 options.
statement: More than 15 options. Use a combo box when there are more than 15 choices in a drop-down list. With so many options, users may find it difficult to navigate with scrolling only.
citation: USWDS. Combo Box — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Combo Box — when to use: Limited space.
statement: Limited space. Use a combo box for presenting options when screen real estate is limited.
citation: USWDS. Combo Box — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — accessibility: Avoid auto-submission.
statement: Avoid auto-submission. Don’t use JavaScript to automatically submit the form (or do anything else) when an option is selected. Auto-submission disrupts screen readers because they select each option as they read them.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — accessibility: Instructions for keyboard navigation
statement: Instructions for keyboard navigation You can navigate this component using the following commands (Mac-equivalent commands are in parentheses):

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — accessibility: Explain unavailable dates and controls.
statement: Explain unavailable dates and controls. Use date restrictions when only some dates are unavailable. Disable the entire picker only when users cannot enter any date, and explain how to make it available.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — accessibility: Choose the appropriate disabled state.
statement: Choose the appropriate disabled state. Native disabled date-picker controls are removed from the tab order. An initialized picker with aria-disabled="true" keeps its visible input and calendar button focusable; USWDS makes the input read-only and prevents the calendar button from opening the calendar.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — implementation: Properties.
statement: Properties. The following properties modify component functionality. These properties can be set or adjusted at any time before or after initialization in order to have an effect.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — implementation: Initialization properties.
statement: Initialization properties. The following properties update the component during initialization. These properties must be set before the component is initialized in order to have an effect.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — implementation: Procedures.
statement: Procedures. The following static procedures update the component after initialization. These are in addition to the primary methods referenced in the JS customization documentation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — implementation: Set the disabled state before initialization.
statement: Set the disabled state before initialization. Add disabled or aria-disabled="true" to the input inside .usa-date-picker. After initialization, use disable, ariaDisable, or enable on the .usa-date-picker element to update both the visible input and calendar button. When switching from native disabled to aria-disabled, call enable before ariaDisable. The native disabled state omits the date value from form submission. The aria-disabled state keeps the date value in form submission.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — usability: Describe the date format.
statement: Describe the date format. Provide a hint of mm/dd/yyyy to help users enter the proper date format if they opt not to use the date picker.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — usability: Always allow a user to type in the date manually.
statement: Always allow a user to type in the date manually. Usability testing suggests some people prefer manually typing the date rather than using the calendar picker. Whenever possible, keep the keyboard active so people can enter in the date information without having to use the picker.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Date Picker — when to consider something else
title: Date Picker — when to consider something else: Familiar dates.
statement: Familiar dates. When asking users for a date they know well, or can look up without using a calendar (like a birthday), use memorable date fields.
citation: USWDS. Date Picker — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Date Picker — when to consider something else
title: Date Picker — when to consider something else: When the day of the week is irrelevant.
statement: When the day of the week is irrelevant. If there's no benefit to knowing the day of the week for a particular date, consider memorable date fields.
citation: USWDS. Date Picker — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — when to use: Scheduling.
statement: Scheduling. When users need to schedule or record an event and benefit from the context of a calendar.
citation: USWDS. Date Picker — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Picker — when to use: When the day of the week is important.
statement: When the day of the week is important. When knowing the day of the week helps users choose a specific date.
citation: USWDS. Date Picker — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — accessibility: Avoid auto-submission.
statement: Avoid auto-submission. Don’t use JavaScript to automatically submit the form (or do anything else) when an option is selected. Auto-submission disrupts screen readers because they select each option as they read them.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — accessibility: Explain unavailable dates and controls.
statement: Explain unavailable dates and controls. Use date restrictions when only some dates are unavailable. If a start or end date cannot be entered, explain why and how to make it available.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — accessibility: Choose the appropriate disabled state for each date picker.
statement: Choose the appropriate disabled state for each date picker. Native disabled controls are removed from the tab order. An initialized date picker with aria-disabled="true" keeps its visible input and calendar button focusable; USWDS makes the input read-only and prevents the calendar button from opening the calendar.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — implementation: Properties.
statement: Properties. The following properties modify component functionality. These properties can be set or adjusted at any time before or after initialization in order to have an effect.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — implementation: Initialization properties.
statement: Initialization properties. The following properties update the component during initialization. These properties must be set before the component is initialized in order to have an effect.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — implementation: Procedures.
statement: Procedures. The following static procedures update the component after initialization. These are in addition to the primary methods referenced in the JS customization documentation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — implementation: Apply disabled states to the individual date pickers.
statement: Apply disabled states to the individual date pickers. Before initialization, put disabled or aria-disabled="true" on each date input that should be unavailable. After initialization, use the date picker procedures on each .usa-date-picker element. When switching a picker from native disabled to aria-disabled, call enable before ariaDisable. Setting an attribute on the .usa-date-range-picker wrapper does not disable its controls. The native disabled state omits that picker’s date value from form submission. The aria-disabled state keeps the date value in form submission.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — usability: Describe the date format.
statement: Describe the date format. Provide a hint of mm/dd/yyyy to help users enter the proper date format if they opt not to use the date picker.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Date Range Picker — usability: Always allow a user to type in the date manually.
statement: Always allow a user to type in the date manually. Usability testing suggests some people prefer manually typing the date rather than using the calendar picker. Whenever possible, keep the keyboard active so people can enter in the date information without having to use the picker.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Date Range Picker — when to consider something else
title: Date Range Picker — when to consider something else: When the day of the week is irrelevant.
statement: When the day of the week is irrelevant. If there's no benefit to knowing the day of the week for a date or range, consider memorable date fields.
citation: USWDS. Date Range Picker — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Date Range Picker — when to use
title: Date Range Picker — when to use: Scheduling.
statement: Scheduling. When users need to schedule or record an event and benefit from the context of a calendar.
citation: USWDS. Date Range Picker — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Date Range Picker — when to use
title: Date Range Picker — when to use: When the day of the week is important.
statement: When the day of the week is important. When knowing the day of the week helps users choose a specific date.
citation: USWDS. Date Range Picker — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — accessibility: Use proper labels and attributes.
statement: Use proper labels and attributes. Each file input should have a label element. Associate the label to your input by defining the value of the label’s for attribute with the input’s id.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — accessibility: Use as a progressive enhancement.
statement: Use as a progressive enhancement. The file input component should be a progressive enhancement of . If the component doesn't initialize, it should still work and appear like a standard file input.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — implementation: Initialization properties.
statement: Initialization properties. JavaScript will create most elements for file input. To get a file input to initialize, add the class name usa-file-input to .

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — implementation: Interaction.
statement: Interaction. When a user selects or drags documents to the file input, the file name and a thumbnail preview are listed.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — implementation: Limit accepted file types with the accept attribute.
statement: Limit accepted file types with the accept attribute. Add the accept attribute to the input element when you want to limit the types of files your input can accept. If a user selects a file that does not match the specified type, the file will not be attached and the file input will display an error message. Learn more about the accept attribute [mozilla.org].

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — implementation: Internet Explorer and older versions of Edge.
statement: Internet Explorer and older versions of Edge. These browsers do not support dragging items to a file input. Instructions to drag files are removed for these browsers.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — implementation: Customizing the error message.
statement: Customizing the error message. Add the data attribute data-errorMessage to usa-file-input to include a custom error message.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — usability: Allow multiple file formats.
statement: Allow multiple file formats. Not everyone has access to the same software. Be flexible with file types to avoid unnecessary software requirements.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — usability: Prefer one file per input.
statement: Prefer one file per input. Some users might not know how to select multiple files in a file browser.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — usability: Use hint text to highlight input restrictions.
statement: Use hint text to highlight input restrictions. Create an element with the usa-hint class to explain any file restrictions, such as document types or file size.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: File Input — when to consider something else
title: File Input — when to consider something else: Documents are optional.
statement: Documents are optional. Avoid asking users to provide documents if you don't require them.
citation: USWDS. File Input — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: File Input — when to consider something else
title: File Input — when to consider something else: Asynchronous upload.
statement: Asynchronous upload. The file input component doesn't support asynchronous uploading. Files will POST only on form submission.
citation: USWDS. File Input — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: File Input — when to consider something else
title: File Input — when to consider something else: Asking for large files.
statement: Asking for large files. Be mindful that some users might have limited connectivity or data plans.
citation: USWDS. File Input — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: File Input — when to use: Documents are required.
statement: Documents are required. Ask users to provide files when it's necessary.
citation: USWDS. File Input — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — accessibility: Use tab focus.
statement: Use tab focus. Code the navigation so that pressing the tab key moves focus from link to link in the navigation, even when the navigation has collapsed into an accordion.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — accessibility: Use accessible accordions.
statement: Use accessible accordions. On small screens: when collapsed into an accordion, the navigation should also meet the accessibility requirements outlined in the "Accordion" section.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — usability: Curate your footer.
statement: Curate your footer. Footer links should point to popular content that might answer a visitor’s remaining questions. Links to disclaimers and legal content sometimes need to be in the footer, but try to minimize “disclaimer bloat” wherever possible.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — usability: The footer doesn’t need to mirror the header.
statement: The footer doesn’t need to mirror the header. Link grouping in the footer does not have to mirror link grouping in top level header navigation (especially if the navigation offers many more links than the footer can).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — usability: Include newsletter signup.
statement: Include newsletter signup. Include the newsletter signup if one of your website’s goals is getting visitors to sign up for a newsletter.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — usability: Avoid stale social media accounts.
statement: Avoid stale social media accounts. Link only to social media your agency updates frequently or uses to communicate with customers.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — usability: Limit contact information to email and phone.
statement: Limit contact information to email and phone. Important contact information should be limited to general email or phone numbers, which should be clickable links to dial from a mobile phone. Physical addresses should live on contact pages users can navigate to from the accordion links.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Footer — when to consider something else
title: Footer — when to consider something else: Medium and slim footers:
statement: Medium and slim footers: Use the big footer when your footer has more than five links.
citation: USWDS. Footer — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — when to use: Big footer:
statement: Big footer: Use the big footer when you want to replicate your site’s navigation scheme in the footer and offer newsletter signups.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — when to use: Medium footer:
statement: Medium footer: Use the medium footer when you want to offer only a few footer links (for disclaimers, terms of service, etc.), social media icons, and contact information.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Footer — when to use: Slim footer:
statement: Slim footer: Use the slim footer when you only want to offer a few footer links and nothing else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — accessibility: Don't rely on the icons alone to convey meaning.
statement: Don't rely on the icons alone to convey meaning. Use text and context to establish the meaning of your list, and use the icon to reinforce that meaning as a progressive enhancement.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — accessibility: Use colors with accessible contrast.
statement: Use colors with accessible contrast. While the icons in an icon list might be considered decorative progressive enhancement, aim for accessible AA contrast. This assures legibility on printed pages as well.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — accessibility: Hide most icons from screen readers.
statement: Hide most icons from screen readers. This component uses the aria-hidden="true" and role=”img” attributes because the icons are used solely as a visual progressive enhancement. The icon's meaning is redundant with the list content.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — accessibility: If you wish to expose icons to screen readers:
statement: If you wish to expose icons to screen readers: - Provide descriptive text for each icon.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — usability: Use consistent headings.
statement: Use consistent headings. Headings should be written with parallel structure. For example, start each with an action verb. When possible, keep headings short enough to fit on one or two lines.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — usability: Add rich content sparingly.
statement: Add rich content sparingly. Each list item can display rich text content like HTML, images, and even other components. Be succinct. Too much complexity distracts from the impact of an icon list.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — usability: Use similar icons.
statement: Use similar icons. Use the same icon for each list item unless variation is meaningful, as with our checkcircle icon ( ) and cancel icon ( ). Icons should come from the same icon library and have a similar look and feel.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Icon List — when to consider something else
title: Icon List — when to consider something else: Multi-step forms or wizards.
statement: Multi-step forms or wizards. The step indicator is best for communicating progress through a form or process that spans several different pages.
citation: USWDS. Icon List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Icon List — when to consider something else
title: Icon List — when to consider something else: Sequential steps.
statement: Sequential steps. Use a standard ordered list or process list if the items must be completed sequentially.
citation: USWDS. Icon List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Icon List — when to consider something else
title: Icon List — when to consider something else: Using complex iconography or graphics.
statement: Using complex iconography or graphics. Use the graphic list if you plan on using different large, complex, or multicolored images with each list item. The icon should only reinforce the text of the list item. If the image needs to convey unique meaning, this is a job for an illustration not an icon.
citation: USWDS. Icon List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Icon List — when to consider something else
title: Icon List — when to consider something else: Improving readability of running text.
statement: Improving readability of running text. The standard unordered list is best for displaying simple lists that are part of running text.
citation: USWDS. Icon List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — when to use: Do-and-don't lists.
statement: Do-and-don't lists. Icon lists help reinforce the message of a list item using a visual cue as a progressive enhancement. This can be effective in a list, or pair of lists, that describe actions users should do or not do. A pair of icons with clear and opposite meaning, like checkcircle () and cancel (), create an effective do-and-don't list.
citation: USWDS. Icon List — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — when to use: Features and metadata.
statement: Features and metadata. Use an icon list to enhance a list of features, like a campsite's amenities or other lists where icons might help users understand content at a glance.
citation: USWDS. Icon List — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — when to use: Important tasks or requirements.
statement: Important tasks or requirements. Use an icon list to help users find, distinguish, and verify related steps or tasks that can be completed in any order, like a checklist of items to pack or documents to complete.
citation: USWDS. Icon List — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon List — when to use: Printable checklists.
statement: Printable checklists. Users may wish to print a page and use it as a physical checklist. This kind of static checklist is not an interactive form. Use an icon like checkboxoutlineblank () to provide a space for physical checking.
citation: USWDS. Icon List — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — accessibility: Hide decorative icons from screen readers.
statement: Hide decorative icons from screen readers. Icons are decorative if they don’t provide meaningful information to the user. Usually, decorative icons are accompanied by text. title: Icon — accessibility: Provide descriptive text if a standalone icon has meaning or provides functionality.
statement: Provide descriptive text if a standalone icon has meaning or provides functionality.
