author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — accessibility: Check for good color contrast.
statement: Check for good color contrast. Make sure that the icon has a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 against its background. See the USWDS color and accessibility page as well as WCAG 2.1 Techniques: Ensuring that a contrast ratio of 3:1 is provided for icons for more information.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — accessibility: Place icons inside links.
statement: Place icons inside links. If icons accompany a text link, place the icon inside the link to prevent screen readers from announcing the link twice.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — implementation: Don’t alter icons.
statement: Don’t alter icons. You shouldn’t customize, combine, or change USWDS icons (other than updating the color) due to their license.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — implementation: Active icons are found in dist/img/usa-icons.
statement: Active icons are found in dist/img/usa-icons. The icons in this directory will be packaged into an SVG sprite. The complete set of available icons are located in two directories: dist/img/material-icons and dist/img/uswds-icons. Copy icons into a usa-icons directory within your project images directory, and rebuild the SVG sprite using uswds-compile.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — implementation: Using color in icons.
statement: Using color in icons. Icons use currentColor, so the color of the icon will be the text color of its parent element. Change colors with the color utility.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — implementation: Relative to font size.
statement: Relative to font size. By default, icons will scale with font size. If you want to specify an icon size, use one of the component’s size variants.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — implementation: Icon names are identifiers.
statement: Icon names are identifiers. To use an icon, simply change the identifier after the pound sign in the sprite path to that icon’s name. For example, to use the accessibilitynew icon, the path will be , or to use the info icon, the path will be .

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — usability: Combine icons with text.
statement: Combine icons with text. Only a few icons are consistently understood across the digital-using public of the world, among them home (), print (), and search (). Combine icons with text to improve clarity, and test your icons for recognition and memorability with your particular audience.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — usability: Be consistent with icon meaning.
statement: Be consistent with icon meaning. Icons used more than once in an application or site must be used to represent the same thing, and have the same text description in every instance. For example, if an icon of a blank piece of paper means “new document” on most screens, choose a different icon to communicate “reformat document.” Consistency helps people with some cognitive disabilities, helps people who might be distracted or scanning, and creates a better user experience for all.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — usability: Combine interactive icons with other components.
statement: Combine interactive icons with other components. If the icon is part of an interactive element, it should be implemented within another functional component. For example, make an icon part of a button or list.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Icon — when to consider something else
title: Icon — when to consider something else: Meaning is ambiguous.
statement: Meaning is ambiguous. Use icons only in a common or conventional way. Icon utility hinges on people quickly recognizing what each icon means. If you suspect that an icon’s intent isn’t perfectly clear, consider removing it or adding accompanying text.
citation: USWDS. Icon — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Icon — when to consider something else
title: Icon — when to consider something else: Compensating for page structure.
statement: Compensating for page structure. Don’t rely on an icon to help draw attention to something important that’s otherwise hard to find. Icons don’t fix unclear page hierarchy or confusing content organization.
citation: USWDS. Icon — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Icon — when to consider something else
title: Icon — when to consider something else: You need illustrative artwork.
statement: You need illustrative artwork. Icons have a specific, functional meaning. Avoid using icons for illustrative purposes. For example, don't use the "visibility" eye icon () to illustrate an actual eye. If you want to enhance the appearance of your content or visually explain a concept, use an illustration instead of an icon.
citation: USWDS. Icon — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — when to use: Draw attention to actions.
statement: Draw attention to actions. Icons, when paired with text, grab attention and show actions to take. Make sure each icon directly relates to any text it accompanies.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — when to use: Help readers find key information.
statement: Help readers find key information. Use icons as scannable, easy-to-understand visual cues for key information, like a phone number or email address.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Icon — when to use: Enhance an actionable target.
statement: Enhance an actionable target. Icons make great touch or click targets. Use an icon for common actions, like opening a menu or sharing an article.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — accessibility: Use proper landmarks for each identifier section.
statement: Use proper landmarks for each identifier section. Each identifier section should be either a section or a nav, and include an appropriate aria-label property.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — accessibility: Add an alt attribute to each logo image.
statement: Add an alt attribute to each logo image. Use [Agency shortname] logo as the alt text for each logo image you add.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — accessibility: Use image role for any SVG images.
statement: Use image role for any SVG images. Use role="img" with any SVG logo image.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Except where noted, use the entire component without deletions or additions.
statement: Except where noted, use the entire component without deletions or additions. With rare exceptions, if you use the identifier, include the entire identifier. That is, don't delete sections or required links or change any link text beyond the customizations mentioned in the implementation section.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Use a background color darker than that of the footer.
statement: Use a background color darker than that of the footer. Anchor the identifier to the bottom of the page and distinguish it from other site content by adding a background color that is darker than the footer. Use primary or base family background colors of grade 80 or higher, or black.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Use an SVG logo if possible.
statement: Use an SVG logo if possible. Ensure the logo is high resolution. We recommend using the SVG version of any logo if you have one. Otherwise, use an image that's at least 120 pixels tall.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Use logos intended for dark backgrounds if possible.
statement: Use logos intended for dark backgrounds if possible. The identifier has a dark background. If your agency has a version of its logo intended for dark backgrounds, use that version.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Update the required links to point to the proper URLs.
statement: Update the required links to point to the proper URLs. The identifier includes links required of any federal website, and these links are specific to a department, agency, or website. We've linked each section below to the guidance on Digital.gov to provide further context.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: [About [Official parent agency acronym]](https://digital.gov/resources/required-web-content-and-links/about-page):
statement: [About [Official parent agency acronym]](https://digital.gov/resources/required-web-content-and-links/about-page): Update the link text to include the parent agency's official acronym. Link to the "About" page of your parent agency's principal website. If your site includes multiple parents, include only the organization highest in the hierarchy in this link.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Accessibility statement:
statement: Accessibility statement: Link to your website or service's accessibility statement, or to your parent agency's accessibility statement if your website or service does not have its own.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: FOIA requests:
statement: FOIA requests: Link to a page that includes information about how the public can request information under the Freedom of Information Act on your parent agency's principal website.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: No FEAR Act data:
statement: No FEAR Act data: Link to the "Equal Employment Opportunity Data Posted Pursuant to the No Fear Act" page on your parent agency's principal website.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Office of the Inspector General:
statement: Office of the Inspector General: Link to your parent agency's Office of the Inspector General.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Performance reports:
statement: Performance reports: Link to a “Budget and Performance” page that includes the parent agency’s strategic plan among other financial and performance documentation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Privacy policy:
statement: Privacy policy: Link to the "Privacy" page most specific to your website. For example, if both your product website and your parent agency's principal website have privacy pages, link to your product website's privacy page here.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Use the Spanish version for Spanish-language sites.
statement: Use the Spanish version for Spanish-language sites. If you have an official Spanish-language website, use the Spanish version of the identifier.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: Duplicate the logo element if using multiple logos.
statement: Duplicate the logo element if using multiple logos. If you're using multiple logos, duplicate the usa-identifierlogo element and link the image to your image source.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — implementation: If applicable, include any taxpayer disclaimer after the standard text.
statement: If applicable, include any taxpayer disclaimer after the standard text. If the organization must provide a taxpayer expense disclaimer, include it following the "Official website" text, as a separate sentence. For example, "An official website of [Department]. Produced and published at taxpayer expense."

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — usability: Use the identifier component for required links.
statement: Use the identifier component for required links. If your site already includes the federally required links in its site footer, remove them in favor of the links in the identifier. This assures that site visitors find the required links in a consistent location from site to site.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — usability: Consider the parent agency the highest-level agency associated with a site or service.
statement: Consider the parent agency the highest-level agency associated with a site or service. In some cases, your site may not have a parent agency. If your site is the primary site for your agency, use your agency name in place of [Parent Agency]. For example, "[agency.gov] An official website of [Agency]."

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — usability: Display the parent agency logo, not the product logo.
statement: Display the parent agency logo, not the product logo. The identifier is meant to identify a website's parent agency as a complement to the site footer. Site-specific logos, like a product logo, should be in the site footer, not the identifier. You may omit the logo in the identifier if it is redundant with the agency logo in your site's footer.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — usability: Display multiple parents and logos in hierarchical order.
statement: Display multiple parents and logos in hierarchical order. If a site has more than one parent agency, you may display a reference and a logo for each parent in hierarchical order, highest first. For example, "An official website of [Grandparent Department] and [Parent Agency]".

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — usability: Avoid distraction.
statement: Avoid distraction. The identifier appears on every page of your site. Choose background colors that fit with your site theme and avoid color combinations that draw excessive attention to the identifier.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — usability: Keep the text up-to-date.
statement: Keep the text up-to-date. Use the most current version of the identifier.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Identifier — when to consider something else
title: Identifier — when to consider something else: Any time it would be misleading.
statement: Any time it would be misleading. The identifier should be used to reduce confusion. Avoid using the identifier on any site meant only for testing or otherwise not meant to be identified as an official government website.
citation: USWDS. Identifier — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Identifier — when to consider something else
title: Identifier — when to consider something else: Redundant content.
statement: Redundant content. Don't add the identifier without removing any duplicate links from your existing site footer. Favor the common links and content in the identifier over any equivalent content in your site footer.
citation: USWDS. Identifier — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — when to use: To identify the highest-level agency associated with a site or service.
statement: To identify the highest-level agency associated with a site or service. The identifier is a complement to the USWDS banner. Use the identifier to tell users what parent agency is responsible for your website. Consider the parent agency the highest-level agency associated with a site or service. If your site is the primary site associated with an agency, you can still use the identifier.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Identifier — when to use: To display links required by federal laws and policies.
statement: To display links required by federal laws and policies. The identifier includes links required on all government sites.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — accessibility: Allow keyboard navigation.
statement: Allow keyboard navigation. Users should be able to navigate between items by using the Tab key. They should also be able to activate a link when pressing Enter on their keyboard. Users should be able to activate hover and focus states with both a mouse and a keyboard.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — accessibility: Keyboard users should access the in-page navigation before the main content.
statement: Keyboard users should access the in-page navigation before the main content. When a user tabs through a page that contains the in-page navigation component, they should find the in-page navigation before the main content. Since the in-page navigation appears after the main content in the reading order, this may seem like a tab-order error. However, tabbing through the entire page before getting to in-page navigation links is not logical, creates confusion, and diminishes the user experience.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — accessibility: Set focus state on section target for keyboard users.
statement: Set focus state on section target for keyboard users. When keyboard users follow an in-page anchor link set the focus state to the link target when the user presses the Enter key. When mouse users follow an in-page anchor link the focus should remain on the selected link.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — implementation: Initialization properties.
statement: Initialization properties. You can customize how the component builds during initialization by adding any of the following properties to the usa-in-page-nav element. These properties must be set before the component is initialized.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — implementation: Custom main content region selector.
statement: Custom main content region selector. The main content selector property (data-main-content-selector) allows you to define which element the component will look in to pull its list of headings. Set the property's value to the class or id of your page's main content region (for example, data-main-content-selector=".main-content" or data-main-content-selector="main-content"). By default, the component will pull headings from the element.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — implementation: Custom heading selector.
statement: Custom heading selector. The heading selector property (data-heading-elements) allows you to list which heading levels you would like the component to pull into the component link list. By default, the component will include h2 and h3 headings.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — implementation: Root margin.
statement: Root margin. The root margin property (data-root-margin) is a string that allows you to define the observable area. This set of values grows or shrinks the observable area from each side of the root element's bounding box before computing intersections. It can accept values similar to the CSS margin property, and can be percentages. By default, the in-page navigation component is set to 0px 0px 0px 0px.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — implementation: Threshold.
statement: Threshold. The threshold property (data-threshold) determines how much of the observable section must be present in the observed area before the nav's item is set to current. The default is 1, which means 100% of the observables must be in the observed section. You can set data-threshold to any integer between 0 and 1.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — references: In-page navigation.
statement: In-page navigation. (2014) Retrieved on August 15, 2022, from https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/page-structure/in-page-navigation/

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — references: Intersection Observer.
statement: Intersection Observer. (July 6, 2022) Retrieved on August 15, 2022, from https://www.w3.org/TR/intersection-observer/

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — references: Intersection Observer API.
statement: Intersection Observer API. (July 23, 2022) Retrieved on August 15, 2022, from https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserverAPI

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — references: IntersectionObserverEntry Interface.
statement: IntersectionObserverEntry Interface. (June 1, 2022) Retrieved on August 15, 2022, from https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserverEntry

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — usability: Display the in-page navigation to the side of the main content.
statement: Display the in-page navigation to the side of the main content. Visually, place the in-page navigation component after the main content in the language’s natural reading order. For example, for a left-to-right language like English, this component goes to the right of the main content.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — usability: Make it stand out.
statement: Make it stand out. Site visitors should be able to quickly and easily distinguish in-page navigation from other landmarks on the page. Include borders and well-defined link active states to clearly convey the utility and purpose of the section. Define a consistent width for the in-page navigation component that is sufficiently wide and does not change based on text length.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — usability: Use language that matches section headings.
statement: Use language that matches section headings. The text of the links displayed within the in-page navigation aside should match the heading text of the target sections. By default, the component scans the page for h2 and h3 elements within the main element, automatically creates the in-page navigation block, and dynamically inserts the text to match the section headings.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — usability: Don't include the page h1 in the navigation.
statement: Don't include the page h1 in the navigation. Each page should have a single h1 to describe its contents. It would be redundant to include this heading level in the in-page navigation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: In Page Navigation — usability: In-page navigation heading.
statement: In-page navigation heading. Inform users that they will scroll down on the same page by including in-page navigation under a descriptive title such as “On this page,” “In this article,” or “Table of contents.”

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: In Page Navigation — when to consider something else
title: In Page Navigation — when to consider something else: Short pages.
statement: Short pages. For pages that require little or no scrolling, in-page navigation is not necessary.
citation: USWDS. In Page Navigation — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: In Page Navigation — when to consider something else
title: In Page Navigation — when to consider something else: Unstructured content.
statement: Unstructured content. Pages that lack heading-based hierarchical structures cannot use the in-page navigation component.
citation: USWDS. In Page Navigation — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: In Page Navigation — when to consider something else
title: In Page Navigation — when to consider something else: Infinite scrolling.
statement: Infinite scrolling. For pages that feature infinite scrolling, in-page navigation is neither a practical nor feasible feature.
citation: USWDS. In Page Navigation — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: In Page Navigation — when to use
title: In Page Navigation — when to use: Long pages.
statement: Long pages. In-page navigation can offer a substantial improvement to user experience for pages that include three or more distinct content sections or content that exceeds three or more viewport heights.
citation: USWDS. In Page Navigation — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Mask — accessibility: Include a label.
statement: Include a label. Make sure each form control includes a label with a for attribute related to the id of the input element it labels.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Mask — accessibility: Use helpful hint text.
statement: Use helpful hint text. Make sure any hint text helps users understand what they need to input.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Mask — accessibility: Customization.
statement: Customization. As you customize, make sure you follow accessibility guidelines for form templates and the accessibility guidelines for form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Mask — usability: Wait to validate.
statement: Wait to validate. Only show error validation messages or stylings after a user has interacted with a particular field.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Input Mask — when to consider something else
title: Input Mask — when to consider something else: When the input requires a free-form field.
statement: When the input requires a free-form field. When there isn’t a common input pattern to use, input masking is not appropriate.
citation: USWDS. Input Mask — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Input Mask — when to consider something else
title: Input Mask — when to consider something else: When the pattern is too complicated to allow for a valid input mask.
statement: When the pattern is too complicated to allow for a valid input mask. A pattern like email, with many possible scenarios for input, is not a good candidate for masking. Allow the user to enter their email address (or other complicated data) and have your validation library confirm before form submission.
citation: USWDS. Input Mask — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Mask — when to use: Common input patterns.
statement: Common input patterns. In fields with a specific expected format like Social Security Number or ZIP code, an input mask allows you to constrain and shape the information being entered into that format, without impairing the user’s ability to copy/paste or correct mistyping.
citation: USWDS. Input Mask — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Prefix Suffix — accessibility: Hide from screen readers.
statement: Hide from screen readers. Prefixes and suffixes are hidden from screen readers using aria-hidden.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Prefix Suffix — accessibility: Use descriptive labels.
statement: Use descriptive labels. Labels should clearly indicate what type of data to enter since prefixes and suffixes are hidden from screen readers. For example, if you’re requesting someone’s height in inches, you have “in.” appear in a suffix, but your form label should say “Height, in inches.”

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Prefix Suffix — implementation: Placement matters.
statement: Placement matters. Place the .usa-input-prefix element before the .usa-input element, and place the .usa-input-suffix element after .usa-input. Both elements should be placed inside .usa-input-group.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Prefix Suffix — implementation: Use text or icons.
statement: Use text or icons. Input prefixes and suffixes can accept either plain text or icons.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Prefix Suffix — implementation: Use validation styles.
statement: Use validation styles. Place input validation classes on usa-input-group.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Prefix Suffix — usability: Follow best practices when using an icon.
statement: Follow best practices when using an icon. If you include an icon as a prefix or suffix, follow the design system’s icon guidance.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Input Prefix Suffix — usability: Use common abbreviations.
statement: Use common abbreviations. Only use commonly understood abbreviations when indicating a text prefix or suffix. Don’t use the full word.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Input Prefix Suffix — when to consider something else
title: Input Prefix Suffix — when to consider something else: Open-ended form fields.
statement: Open-ended form fields. If there aren’t specific parameters around the information the user needs to enter, a prefix or suffix may be incorrect. For example, don’t use a $ prefix for a form field asking “What’s a fair resolution?” if the user could enter either “$1,000” or “a full refund” as the answer.
citation: USWDS. Input Prefix Suffix — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Input Prefix Suffix — when to consider something else
title: Input Prefix Suffix — when to consider something else: Explanation requires additional words.
statement: Explanation requires additional words. Don’t use prefixes or suffixes if a symbol or abbreviation is insufficient to convey the meaning. There shouldn’t be any confusion between what type of information a prefix or suffix represents. This is especially true when using icons that could have multiple meanings.
citation: USWDS. Input Prefix Suffix — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Input Prefix Suffix — when to use
title: Input Prefix Suffix — when to use: Highlight the type of information.
statement: Highlight the type of information. Prefixes and suffixes are useful when there’s a commonly understood symbol or abbreviation for the type of information the user needs to enter. Some common examples include units of measurement (like lbs or ft), symbols (like $ or %), or even icons (like showing an eye for password visibility).
citation: USWDS. Input Prefix Suffix — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Input Prefix Suffix — when to use
title: Input Prefix Suffix — when to use: Input cannot include units.
statement: Input cannot include units. Use prefixes and suffixes if the input refers to a unit or currency amount (like a length or dollar amount), but the user's input must include digits only, not units or a currency symbol.
citation: USWDS. Input Prefix Suffix — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Input Prefix Suffix — when to use
title: Input Prefix Suffix — when to use: Reduce mental load.
statement: Reduce mental load. Adding a prefix or suffix can help the user more quickly understand what kind of information is requested.
citation: USWDS. Input Prefix Suffix — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — accessibility: Allow keyboard navigation of links.
statement: Allow keyboard navigation of links. Users should be able to navigate between links by using the “Tab” key. They should be able to activate a link by pressing the “Enter” key.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — accessibility: Link hover state should be visible on focus.
statement: Link hover state should be visible on focus. Users should be able to activate hover and focus states with both a mouse and a keyboard.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — overview: Link — overview
statement: Each item below is explained in the guidance sections that follow. What you should do Clearly identify external links Notify users about non-federal external links Use unique, meaningful link text Simplify link placement in body text Link directly to the most relevant page Indicate nonpublic links that require authentication If you use an external link indicator, use it consistently for all text links Add rel="noreferrer" to external links Provide text context for external links Add a non-endorsement statement Indicate file type and size for links to non-HTML content Identify jump links in body text Write out email and phone links Encode email and phone links Check with your IT security department regarding email link best practices What you shouldn't do Don’t rely only on color to distinguish links Don’t block external links with disruptive notifications Don’t use generic link text like “read more” or “link” Don’t use the same link text for different URLs on the same page

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — research findings: Qualitative comparison A/B test of external link indicator:
statement: Qualitative comparison A/B test of external link indicator: In May–June 2021, USWDS conducted research around using an external link indicator for text links to external websites. We first performed a landscape analysis of commonly used external link icons and designed an alternative variant of the external link indicator. Then, we conducted a qualitative comparison A/B usability test of our default external link icon and a newly designed “Exit” badge. Our findings:

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should not: Don’t rely on only color to distinguish links.
statement: Don’t rely on only color to distinguish links. Site visitors should be able to distinguish text links from surrounding text. In most cases, include an underline or bottom border on text links, in addition to a consistent link color. Text links not distinguished with an underline need a contrast level of at least 3:1 with their surrounding text (the same as AA Large, or a USWDS magic number of 40) and should show an underline on hover.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should not: Don't block external links with disruptive notifications.
statement: Don't block external links with disruptive notifications. Allow users to follow external links without taking a separate action to acknowledge leaving your site. Roadblock notices, such as modals and dialog boxes, result in a poor user experience. Instead, communicate about a link’s destination through descriptive link text and external link indicators. Use your site’s policy and notices page to provide important information about non-government sites without disrupting the user experience.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should not: Don’t use generic link text.
statement: Don’t use generic link text. Vague text like “click here” and “read more” is confusing and repetitive, especially to people using screen readers. Link text should describe the destination and explain where users will go if they follow the link.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should not: Don’t use the same link text for different URLs on the same page.
statement: Don’t use the same link text for different URLs on the same page. Differentiate between links by using unique text for each.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Clearly identify external links.
statement: Clearly identify external links. The external link icon ( ) is a good way to communicate that a link is external.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Notify users about non-federal links.
statement: Notify users about non-federal links. Review this resource on Digital.gov for guidance on non-federal link requirements.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Use unique, meaningful link text.
statement: Use unique, meaningful link text. Link text should explain the link's purpose and help the user understand the link's destination. Vague and repetitive text like “click here” or “read more” is unhelpful to those using screen-reading software. Screen-reading software collects all page links into a single list, and users typically start with that list. When they do so, they will not be able to tell the difference between links with similar wording.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Simplify link placement in body text.
statement: Simplify link placement in body text. A link requires mental effort, which affects readability. Reduce the number of links in a single sentence to simplify its message. Consider placing links at the beginning or end of sentences to improve readability.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Link directly to the most relevant page.
statement: Link directly to the most relevant page. Avoid links to pages that require further user action to locate the intended information.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Indicate nonpublic links that require authentication.
statement: Indicate nonpublic links that require authentication. Use text or an indicator like a lock icon to signal any link that is not available publicly. This includes links behind a login or other authentication like a paywall.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: If you use an external link indicator, use it consistently for all external text links.
statement: If you use an external link indicator, use it consistently for all external text links. If your project uses an external link indicator (like an icon), use that indicator for all text links across your site. If users learn to associate an external link with the indicator, they will also appropriately expect that text links without an indicator are not external links. Icon- or image-only links like social share buttons or logos do not need the same treatment as text links.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Use rel="noreferrer" property on external links.
statement: Use rel="noreferrer" property on external links. Setting noreferrer on links prevents the browser from leaking information about the original web address.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Provide text context for external links.
statement: Provide text context for external links. Following a link is a user decision. Users need enough information to make that decision - short links without context often don’t provide that. Plain, straightforward text can be the best way to communicate to users that a link will take them away from your site, which can be useful whether the external link is to either a government or a non-government site. When possible, use the content of the link text itself to indicate where it goes. By itself, an external link indicator (like an icon) can be ambiguous. Adding plain text can help make any link destination more clear.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Add a non-endorsement statement to your site.
statement: Add a non-endorsement statement to your site. Your “Policy and Notices” page should explain to users that your agency does not endorse the information on any linked non-federal site. See, for example, USA.gov’s linking policy. In addition to this site-level notice, consider adding additional non-endorsement statements on individual pages with non-federal links.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Indicate file type and size for links to non-HTML content.
statement: Indicate file type and size for links to non-HTML content. Whenever possible, create HTML pages instead of linking to files like PDFs. If you do link to a file, tell users ahead of time if the link may trigger a file download, and show the size and format of that file.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Identify jump links in body text.
statement: Identify jump links in body text. Jump links (or in-page links) send the user to another part of the same page. This behavior can be unexpected in body text links. In these cases, use the link text like "jump to", "above" or "below" to tell users that the destination is elsewhere on the same page.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Write out email and phone links.
statement: Write out email and phone links. For mailto: and tel: links, write out email addresses and phone numbers so users can read or copy this information without selecting the link.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Encode email and phone links.
statement: Encode email and phone links. Some browsers don’t automatically display a clickable link for email addresses or phone numbers, so encode email and phone links with mailto: and tel:. Be sure to include the country code in phone numbers to support international users.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Link — usability should: Check with your IT security department regarding email link best practices.
statement: Check with your IT security department regarding email link best practices. While displaying email addresses and phone numbers provides a better experience for users, it can also increase spam for the email recipient. One approach is to use a group email address to protect individuals. Another benefit of that approach is the email will remain the same even as staff and organizational structures change. You can also consider using a contact form instead of showing email addresses.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: List — implementation: Remove list styles with the unstyled variant.
statement: Remove list styles with the unstyled variant. For unstyled lists, either add the .usa-list--unstyled class or use the Sass mixin: @include unstyled-list.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: List — usability: Use sentence case and begin lists with a capital letter.
statement: Use sentence case and begin lists with a capital letter. - Use punctuation appropriate to the text. Do not leave sentences without periods.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: List — when to consider something else
title: List — when to consider something else: If you need to communicate long lists of narrative text.
statement: If you need to communicate long lists of narrative text.
citation: USWDS. List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: List — when to use: Ordered list:
statement: Ordered list: Use an ordered list when you need to display text in some ranking, hierarchy, or series of steps.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: List — when to use: Unordered list:
statement: Unordered list: Use unordered lists to display text in no specific order.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Memorable Date — accessibility: Follow input guidance.
statement: Follow input guidance. These text fields should follow the accessibility guidelines for all text inputs.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Memorable Date — accessibility: Don’t auto-advance focus.
statement: Don’t auto-advance focus. Do not use JavaScript to auto advance the focus from one field to the next. This makes it difficult for keyboard-only users to navigate and correct mistakes.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Memorable Date — accessibility: Use "text" instead of "number" inputs.
statement: Use "text" instead of "number" inputs. Research indicates that numeric inputs still carry many usability problems, according to the gov.uk Technology in Government blog.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Memorable Date — implementation: Memorable Date — implementation
statement: - The year input is set to accept only a four-digit number while the month and day inputs can accept up to a two-digit number. - Always use back-end validation on dates for correctness.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Memorable Date — related: Memorable Date — related
statement: - Date of Birth pattern - Phone Number pattern - Social Security Number pattern

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Memorable Date — usability: Label each field.
statement: Label each field. Be sure each field is properly labeled — some countries enter dates in day, month, year order

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Memorable Date — usability: Avoid select elements for day or year.
statement: Avoid select elements for day or year. It may be tempting to switch all or some of these text fields to select elements, but these tend to be more difficult to use than text inputs.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Memorable Date — when to consider something else
title: Memorable Date — when to consider something else: Consider a date picker for scheduling.
statement: Consider a date picker for scheduling. If users are trying to schedule something, the date picker might make more sense. Be sure to also provide an option for text entry as well.
citation: USWDS. Memorable Date — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Memorable Date — when to use: Appropriate for most dates.
statement: Appropriate for most dates. This component is appropriate for most dates.
citation: USWDS. Memorable Date — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — accessibility: Label the modal with its heading.
statement: Label the modal with its heading. Use aria-labelledby=”[id]” on .usa-modal to read out the modal title when opening the modal. The [id] should match the value of the id attribute on the usa-modalheading element.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — accessibility: Share more context with aria-describedby.
statement: Share more context with aria-describedby. Optionally, you may also use aria-describedby=”[id]” on .usa-modal to associate descriptive text to the modal window so that it’s read when opening the modal. The id should belong to a paragraph or a brief piece of content.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — accessibility: Include the “X” close button at the end of the modal code.
statement: Include the “X” close button at the end of the modal code. CSS will display .usa-modalclose at the top right of the modal window, but placing the close button at the bottom of the modal will prevent some screen readers from reading the close button first and allow users to navigate directly to the main content instead.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — accessibility: Ensure keyboard focus is trapped inside the modal.
statement: Ensure keyboard focus is trapped inside the modal. When using a keyboard to test the modal, ensure focus does not move to the page behind it.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — implementation: Use unique ids.
statement: Use unique ids. Each .usa-modal must have a unique id so that openers can associate them with their aria-controls attribute.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — implementation: Openers.
statement: Openers. A single modal can have multiple openers. Each opener requires data-open-modal and aria-controls=”[modalid]” attributes. Openers can be coded as either or elements. Using helps link to modals in the event JavaScript fails.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — implementation: Closers.
statement: Closers. Place a data-close-modal attribute on any button that will close a modal. Closers may have event listeners attached to them. Code closers as .

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — implementation: Disabling close when an action is required.
statement: Disabling close when an action is required. In instances that a user must make a choice before continuing, you want to prevent them from closing the modal without taking action. Add data-force-action attribute to .usa-modal to prevent the user from closing the modal without taking an action.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — usability: Users should trigger modals.
statement: Users should trigger modals. Modals should appear as a result of an action made by the user or (less commonly) inactivity. A modal should not surprise the user, so don’t automatically display them. Some exceptions would be to alert the user that their authenticated session in a web application is about to expire due to inactivity or if information needs to be displayed when arriving at a webpage for the first time (like accepting the use of cookies).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — usability: Choose the modal size that fits your content.
statement: Choose the modal size that fits your content. There are two sizes to choose from: default and large. If a modal’s content can’t fit without scrolling, you may need to use the large variant or consider moving the content to its own page.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — usability: Use clear header and button text.
statement: Use clear header and button text. The header should clearly state what’s happening or what action the modal is prompting the user to do. The button text should indicate what will happen when selected and avoid ambiguity. For example, if a modal asks “Do you want to cancel?” the button options should not be “yes” and “cancel” — instead use something like “Yes, cancel” and “No, don’t cancel.”

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — usability: Limit in-modal interactions.
statement: Limit in-modal interactions. Avoid using components other than buttons inside the modal. Components such as accordions and form fields often don’t scale well for mobile users and they can easily lose context that they’re viewing a modal. If you need to include links that navigate away from a modal to another webpage, refer to our link guidance about how to handle external links.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — usability: Consider what happens when the modal is dismissed.
statement: Consider what happens when the modal is dismissed. The page underneath should not reload or change to new content.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — usability: Avoid long content that requires scrolling.
statement: Avoid long content that requires scrolling. If a lot of content is needed, make sure it’s clear that users have to scroll to see all of it. Lengthy content can be problematic because it pushes buttons out of a user’s initial view, which may cause confusion.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — usability: Don't roadblock external links with a modal window or dialog box.
statement: Don't roadblock external links with a modal window or dialog box. Allow users to follow external links without taking a separate action to acknowledge leaving your site. Roadblock notices result in a poor user experience and are redundant with both the link's destination context and your site's policies and notices page (see Link guidance).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Modal — when to consider something else
title: Modal — when to consider something else: Every time!
statement: Every time! Before using a modal, consider whether there’s another component that might be less disruptive for the user. Modals should be a last resort.
citation: USWDS. Modal — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Modal — when to consider something else
title: Modal — when to consider something else: Multi-step process.
statement: Multi-step process. Avoid complicated user flows in a modal that may take the user away from the original page. A multi-step process is better suited to an individual page, guiding the user and accommodating complexities in the user flow.
citation: USWDS. Modal — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Modal — when to consider something else
title: Modal — when to consider something else: Error, success, or warning messages.
statement: Error, success, or warning messages. When these relate to a form field, these are better displayed in the context of the page (such as showing an error next to a missing required field). When these relate to page-level messages (such as confirming that a form has been successfully submitted), they should appear as an alert at the top of the page where the user is taken next.
citation: USWDS. Modal — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — when to use: Confirmation.
statement: Confirmation. Use modals to force the user to complete a task or make a decision that requires their full attention outside of the main workflow. These modals are usually triggered by a user action on the page and offer more than one option to proceed — such as a “yes” and “no” button. They are commonly used to confirm user actions or tasks that can’t be undone.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — when to use: Acknowledgement before continuing.
statement: Acknowledgement before continuing. These modals are used as a “gate” to prevent users from moving forward without acknowledging or answering specific information in the modal. A key differentiator of these modals is that a user should not be able to close the modal or escape without making a selection — this means the “close” button should be disabled on these modals. It also means there needs to be a clear way to accept or reject the content in the modal.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Modal — when to use: Explanatory content without disrupting a process.
statement: Explanatory content without disrupting a process. A modal can be used to display information without taking users away from a process or task. These modals usually show optional information to help a user gain further understanding about what they’re doing — for instance, displaying a privacy policy while creating an account or viewing an in-depth definition or explanation while filling out a form. Typically these modals don’t require a user to take action other than closing it.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — accessibility: Use the element.
statement: Use the element. Use a wrapping element to identify Pagination as a navigation section to screen readers and other assistive technologies.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — accessibility: Use a unique, descriptive ARIA label for the element.
statement: Use a unique, descriptive ARIA label for the element. Provide a descriptive ARIA label for any Pagination component's element that describes its purpose. For example, if the pagination component is used to navigate through a set of search results, an appropriate label could be aria-label="search results page". If you use more than one Pagination component on a page, each will need a unique ARIA label.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — accessibility: Use an unordered list for the navigation items.
statement: Use an unordered list for the navigation items. This allows screen readers to voice the number of elements in the Pagination component

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — accessibility: Voice the current page.
statement: Voice the current page. Use aria-current="page" on the current page's link item to properly voice the current page for screen readers.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — accessibility: Voice the word "page" before the page numbers in links.
statement: Voice the word "page" before the page numbers in links. Use aria-label="page []" on each page link to be explicit that the numbers are links to page numbers.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — accessibility: Voice "last page" on the last page's link in a bounded set.
statement: Voice "last page" on the last page's link in a bounded set. Use aria-label="last page, page []" to voice that the last element in the navigation is the last page in the paginated section. Don't include this on the last navigation element in an unbounded set, since there is no last page in an unbounded set.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — accessibility: Use a link for the current page for robustness.
statement: Use a link for the current page for robustness. While it may sound counterintuitive to link to the current page in your Pagination component, it makes sense to include this as a link so screen readers voice the current page whether the user navigates by element or by tabbing.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — accessibility: Avoid large horizontal gaps between elements.
statement: Avoid large horizontal gaps between elements. Users with limited vision or mobility may stop scanning and miss an element if there's too much horizontal space between it and the previous element in the reading order.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — implementation: Set the current page item.
statement: Set the current page item. Use the usa-current class to highlight the currently active page.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — implementation: Pair with the Collection component.
statement: Pair with the Collection component. To display related items like articles or events in a compact list, consider using Pagination with the Collection component, which offers short descriptions and then directs users to the original source.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — implementation: Bounded and unbounded sets.
statement: Bounded and unbounded sets. The USWDS Pagination component is designed to work with both paginated sets that have a discrete number of pages (most paginated content) and those that do not. Bounded sets have a discrete number of pages and each page is potentially equally relevant (such as a set of blog posts sorted chronologically). Unbounded sets (often returned as a search result) are large sets sorted by relevance, where deeper pages have less relevance. Unbounded sets show no last page.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — usability: Show the size of the paginated set.
statement: Show the size of the paginated set. Users want to know the length of a paginated section. This is most commonly accomplished by always showing the last page as the last item in the pagination navigation. Users should also know if the set is unbounded and has no discrete length. For example, some large search results will not have a "last" page. The USWDS Pagination component will always show the last page of the set as a navigable link, or show an ellipsis at the end of the links if the set is unbounded.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — usability: Highlight the current page.
statement: Highlight the current page. Pagination shows the current page the user is on in relation to the entire collection of pages.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — usability: Always include the first, previous, and next pages.
statement: Always include the first, previous, and next pages. Users should always be able to navigate to each of these pages from any page in the set.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — usability: Show navigation items in a single line.
statement: Show navigation items in a single line. Pagination can be hard to understand — and individual items can be more difficult to select — when the items break over one line. Don't split the navigation items over multiple lines. Avoid using Pagination in any context where it would be more than one line long.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — usability: Indicate any missing pages.
statement: Indicate any missing pages. Don't include out-of-sequence items directly adjacent to one another. Whenever there are pages missing — either between two elements, or at the end of an unbounded sequence — indicate the missing pages with an indicator like a non-selectable ellipsis.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — usability: Use as few navigation items as possible.
statement: Use as few navigation items as possible. Showing more pages than necessary tends to add complexity and use more space without proportional increases to the component's functionality. Focus on the essential actions and avoid adding more items to Pagination just to fill space.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — usability: Use generous touch targets.
statement: Use generous touch targets. Use touch targets that are big enough to select with any finger and have enough separation to avoid mistakes.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — usability: Optimize the number of entries per page.
statement: Optimize the number of entries per page. Consider page load, performance, and the user's scrolling preferences when determining how many items are displayed on each page. Some paginated content benefits from user control over the number of elements to show on each page.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Pagination — when to consider something else
title: Pagination — when to consider something else: Meaningful page groupings.
statement: Meaningful page groupings. If you have long content split meaningfully, or grouped by subject or theme, use conventional navigation like Side navigation.
citation: USWDS. Pagination — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Pagination — when to consider something else
title: Pagination — when to consider something else: Steps in a sequence.
statement: Steps in a sequence. If you need to indicate progress in a series of steps that must be completed in succession, like an onboarding flow, consider using the step indicator component.
citation: USWDS. Pagination — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Pagination — when to consider something else
title: Pagination — when to consider something else: Short collections.
statement: Short collections. If the length of the entire collection is less than 3-4 screen lengths long, consider showing all the items at once instead of paginating.
citation: USWDS. Pagination — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — when to use: Search results.
statement: Search results. Pagination is most commonly used with paginated search results. Our Pagination component is designed to work both with results that have a discrete number of results pages (bounded) and those with an uncalculated number of results pages (unbounded). See Using the Pagination component, below, for more on bounded and unbounded sets.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Pagination — when to use: Multi-page collections of related items.
statement: Multi-page collections of related items. Splitting a large collection of related items into individual pages can improve browsability and scannability. Common examples of multi-page collections include articles related to a category or tag, content archives, and history or activity.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — accessibility: Use semantic heading levels.
statement: Use semantic heading levels. Though our default code uses an , use the correct heading level with the class name usa-process-listheading in your own implementation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: Use counters to reinforce step progression.
statement: Use counters to reinforce step progression. The counter pattern (step numbers in a circle) attracts more attention to the indicator bar, but more strongly communicates step-by-step progression. Use counters when you want to reinforce step progression. Omit them if testing proves that this reinforcement is unnecessary for your audience.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: Omit labels with verbose content.
statement: Omit labels with verbose content. Aim for clear and crisp labels. Omit labels to save space or if the step names are too long to comfortably fit in the step indicator.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: Use the centered variant with centered content and headings.
statement: Use the centered variant with centered content and headings. The centered variant is designed to complement centered content and headings. If you have left-aligned content and headings, use the default alignment.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: Center the heading with utilities.
statement: Center the heading with utilities. Use the flex-justify-center utility on usa-step-indicatorheader to center the heading.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: Centered counters need narrower gaps and a thinner segment.
statement: Centered counters need narrower gaps and a thinner segment. If you use a centered variant with counters, you should use a narrower gap (2px is a good starting point) to increase the continuity between segments. A narrower counter gap (again, 2px is a good starting point) can also improve legibility. Centered counters can also benefit from a thinner segment, as the centered variant focusses emphasis on the counter instead of the segment.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: Pending text should use gray.
statement: Pending text should use gray. Pending text should use the gray family that complements the background and the pending segment colors. Use warm grays with warm backgrounds and segments, and cool grays with cool backgrounds and segments.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: Pending segments can use gray or complete family.
statement: Pending segments can use gray or complete family. Pending segments can use gray, just as with pending text, but they can also use a light grade of the complete color family.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: The current color can be a contrast color.
statement: The current color can be a contrast color. The current color can be in the same family as the complete color or it can be a contrast color that distinguishes itself from the complete color.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: Thicker segments use wider counter gaps.
statement: Thicker segments use wider counter gaps. It can be distracting to use a thick segment with a narrow counter gap. Use a gap of at least 0.5 units on a 1 unit segment.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — implementation: Avoid wide counter gaps.
statement: Avoid wide counter gaps. Counter gaps cap improve legibility of the counters, but wide counter gaps hurt the overall continuity between the counters and the segments.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — usability: Be thoughtful about the number of steps.
statement: Be thoughtful about the number of steps. A process list should include between three and ten steps to prevent it from getting too unwieldy or confusing.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — usability: Use consistent headings.
statement: Use consistent headings. Headings should be written with a parallel structure (e.g., all start with an action verb, etc.), including consistent end punctuation, and should be short enough to fit on one line, if possible.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — usability: Add other types of content as needed.
statement: Add other types of content as needed. The body of each list item can be used to display additional rich text content including HTML, images, and other components like buttons, images, simple lists, links, and tables.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Process List — when to consider something else
title: Process List — when to consider something else: Multi-page forms or wizards.
statement: Multi-page forms or wizards. Use the step indicator component to help users work through a form or process that spans several different pages.
citation: USWDS. Process List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Process List — when to consider something else
title: Process List — when to consider something else: When showing current status or progress.
statement: When showing current status or progress. Use the step indicator component to show the user the current step in a multi-step process.
citation: USWDS. Process List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Process List — when to consider something else
title: Process List — when to consider something else: In-page navigation.
statement: In-page navigation. Use the side navigation component to display the “sub-navigation” within a section or page of the website.
citation: USWDS. Process List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Process List — when to consider something else
title: Process List — when to consider something else: The steps are non-sequential.
statement: The steps are non-sequential. Use unordered lists, graphic lists (coming soon), or icon lists (coming soon) to display text that doesn’t have a clear, logical order to it.
citation: USWDS. Process List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Process List — when to consider something else
title: Process List — when to consider something else: The listed content is meant to improve readability of a complex sentence.
statement: The listed content is meant to improve readability of a complex sentence. Use the ordered and unordered list components to break up sentences and paragraphs with lists. These lists are part of the general content of the page and don’t need the typographical hierarchy or visual impact of the process list.
citation: USWDS. Process List — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Process List — when to use: Displaying high-level sequential steps.
statement: Displaying high-level sequential steps. Use process lists to create a clear hierarchy and help users easily differentiate between individual steps or stages in a process.
citation: USWDS. Process List — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Prose — implementation: Prose — implementation
statement: - usa-prose is meant for blocks of text where it’s more difficult to add custom classes to individual elements, like a blog post where the content is coming out of markdown or a CMS. - Adding usa-prose to any container adds USWDS default heading and body text styling to the following direct-child elements: - h1-h6 - p - ul and ol, plus child li - table, plus child thead, th, td, and caption - Customize line-length by changing the value of $theme-text-measure and $theme-lead-measure in your USWDS settings configuration. Each setting accepts a measure token. - $theme-text-measure - $theme-lead-measure

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — accessibility: Use fieldset and legend.
statement: Use fieldset and legend. Group related radio buttons together with and describe the group with .

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — accessibility: Use proper labels and attributes.
statement: Use proper labels and attributes. Each radio button should have a . Associate the two by matching the ’s for attribute to the ’s id attribute.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — usability: Use the label as a target.
statement: Use the label as a target. Users should be able to select either the text label or the radio button to select or deselect an option.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — usability: List items vertically.
statement: List items vertically. Vertically-listed options are easier to read than those that are listed horizontally. A horizontal layout can make it difficult to tell which label belongs to which radio button.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — usability: Use adequate spacing.
statement: Use adequate spacing. Make sure selections are adequately spaced for touch screens. Consider using the tile variant for larger touch targets.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — usability: Set default values with caution.
statement: Set default values with caution. Setting a default value can bias a decision, seem pushy, or alienate users who don’t fit your assumptions. Only use a default selection if you have data to back it up.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — usability: Don’t mix default and tile variants.
statement: Don’t mix default and tile variants. Pick one implementation and stick with it. When mixed, tiles can appear to indicate a bias or preference toward that option.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — usability: Use a logical order.
statement: Use a logical order. Make sure the selection options are organized in a meaningful way, like alphabetical or most-frequent to least-frequent. This helps users easily find the option they’re looking for.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Radio Buttons — when to consider something else
title: Radio Buttons — when to consider something else: Multiple selections.
statement: Multiple selections. If users need to select more than one option or if there’s only one item to select, use checkboxes instead.
citation: USWDS. Radio Buttons — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Radio Buttons — when to consider something else
title: Radio Buttons — when to consider something else: Limited space.
statement: Limited space. Consider a select component if you don’t have enough space to list out all available options.
citation: USWDS. Radio Buttons — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Radio Buttons — when to consider something else
title: Radio Buttons — when to consider something else: Selecting none.
statement: Selecting none. If users should be able to select zero of the options or change their mind and unselect an option, consider using checkboxes. You can also choose to add a “none of the above” option to the radio button group instead.
citation: USWDS. Radio Buttons — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Radio Buttons — when to use: To display a single selection.
statement: To display a single selection. When users need to select only one option from a set of mutually exclusive choices.
citation: USWDS. Radio Buttons — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Range Slider — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Range Slider — implementation: Range Slider — implementation
statement: - Set the min and max attribute of the input element to correspond to the instructions or labels that accompany the slider.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Range Slider — references: Range Slider — references
statement: - Slider Design: Rules of Thumb [Nielsen Norman Group] - Four Dangerous Navigation Approaches that Can Increase Cognitive Strain [Nielsen Norman Group; See example 4]

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Range Slider — usability: Highlight the control when selected.
statement: Highlight the control when selected. The slider control should change color to indicate it is active when a user selects it.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Range Slider — usability: The control must be draggable.
statement: The control must be draggable. Users should be able to drag the slider control or select somewhere along the slider itself to change the value.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Range Slider — usability: Label the limits of the range.
statement: Label the limits of the range. When appropriate, label the ends of the slider with the limits of the range (for example: “0/100”, “small/large” or “less expensive/more expensive”).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Range Slider — usability: Don’t be too granular.
statement: Don’t be too granular. In a range slider, the relative value is more important than the specific value, so set the step attribute so it’s not too granular. By setting the step to a value of 10-20% of the total range you prevent unnecessary precision and cognitive strain in your users. For example, set step="10" in a total range of 100.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Range Slider — when to consider something else
title: Range Slider — when to consider something else: Range Slider — when to consider something else
statement: - Use a regular text input if a user needs to enter a precise number.
citation: USWDS. Range Slider — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Range Slider — when to use: When the range is more important than precision.
statement: When the range is more important than precision. For instance, it could be more important for a target price selector to communicate where the target price falls within a certain range than the precise dollar amount selected.
citation: USWDS. Range Slider — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Range Slider — when to use: When a relative value is more important than an exact value.
statement: When a relative value is more important than an exact value. For instance, a volume slider is typically more focussed on the relative loudness of the output rather than the specific decibel level.
citation: USWDS. Range Slider — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — accessibility: Include the word “Search” in the button.
