statement: Include the word “Search” in the button. Always include the word “search” inside the element for screen readers. You can visually hide this text using the CSS class usa-sr-only or Sass mixin @include sr-only.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — usability: Make the input at least 27 characters wide.
statement: Make the input at least 27 characters wide. Allow the search component to be as wide as possible, but a minimum of 27 characters wide. This allows users to enter multiple search terms and still be able to see all of them. The more users can see their search terms, the easier it is to review, verify, and submit their search query. Romance languages are about 20% longer than English, so account for text swell on multilingual websites.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — usability: The magnifying glass icon is effective.
statement: The magnifying glass icon is effective. The magnifying glass has been shown to be almost universally recognized by users as an indicator of search, and doesn’t need to be visually paired with the word "Search" as long as it remains for screen readers.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — usability: Search terms should persist into search results.
statement: Search terms should persist into search results. When displaying the search results, preload the search bar content with the original search terms.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — usability: Use a full search box on the home page.
statement: Use a full search box on the home page. On a site’s home page the search function should appear as a search box instead of a link so users can locate it easily.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — usability: Don’t offer advanced search as the default.
statement: Don’t offer advanced search as the default. The majority of people will do a simple search with one or two search terms. If advanced search is offered, it increases the likelihood of mistakes.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — usability: Use a label even if it’s visually hidden.
statement: Use a label even if it’s visually hidden. The form field should include a label for screen reader users.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — usability: The search button should be a submit button.
statement: The search button should be a submit button. This reduces the number of keystrokes required to use the form.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Search — when to consider something else
title: Search — when to consider something else: Very small sites.
statement: Very small sites. On single-page or very small sites, you may be able to get away without a search bar.
citation: USWDS. Search — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Search — when to use: Use site search.
statement: Use site search. There will always be users who would benefit from being able to search your site.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Select — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Select — accessibility: Always use a label.
statement: Always use a label. Make sure your select element has a label. Don’t replace it with the default menu option (for example, removing the “State” label and just having the menu read “Select a state” by default).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Select — accessibility: Avoid auto-submission.
statement: Avoid auto-submission. Don’t use JavaScript to automatically submit the form (or do anything else) when an option is selected. Auto-submission disrupts screen readers because they select each option as they read them.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Select — usability: Make sure to test.
statement: Make sure to test. Test select menus thoroughly with members of your target audience. Several usability experts suggest they should be the “UI of last resort.” Many users find them confusing and difficult to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Select — usability: Avoid dependent options.
statement: Avoid dependent options. Avoid making options in one select menu change based on the input to another. Users often don’t understand how choosing an item in one impacts another.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Select — usability: Use a good default.
statement: Use a good default. When most users will (or should) pick a particular option, make it the default: Default

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Select — usability: Avoid auto-submission.
statement: Avoid auto-submission. Don’t use JavaScript to automatically submit the form (or do anything else) when an option is chosen. Offer a “submit” button at the end of the form instead. Users often change their choices multiple times. Auto-submission is also less accessible.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Select — when to consider something else
title: Select — when to consider something else: Fewer than seven options.
statement: Fewer than seven options. Use radio buttons instead.
citation: USWDS. Select — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Select — when to consider something else
title: Select — when to consider something else: More than 15 options.
statement: More than 15 options. If the list of options is very long, consider using a combo box.
citation: USWDS. Select — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Select — when to consider something else
title: Select — when to consider something else: Multi-select.
statement: Multi-select. If you need to allow users to choose more than one option at once. Users often don’t understand how to choose multiple items from select elements. Use checkboxes instead.
citation: USWDS. Select — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Select — when to consider something else
title: Select — when to consider something else: Site navigation.
statement: Site navigation. Use the navigation components instead.
citation: USWDS. Select — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Select — when to use: Use sparingly.
statement: Use sparingly. Use the select component only when a user needs to choose from about seven to 15 possible options and you have limited space to display the options.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Sidenav — accessibility: Sidenav — accessibility
statement: - The width of the current menu item’s highlight border is set with the $theme-sidenav-current-border-width variable.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Sidenav — usability: Show the current page.
statement: Show the current page. Indicate where a user is within the navigational hierarchy. Use the “active” state to show users which page they have navigated to.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Sidenav — usability: Keep the navigation links short.
statement: Keep the navigation links short. They can be shorter derivatives of page titles themselves.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Sidenav — usability: Always test your navigation.
statement: Always test your navigation. If the navigation hierarchy is too long, users may miss items at the bottom. If it’s too deep, users may miss items that require too many clicks. Usability test to find the right balance between breadth and depth.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Sidenav — when to consider something else
title: Sidenav — when to consider something else: Small site.
statement: Small site. If the site has fewer than five pages, consider organizing the page without a navigational hierarchy.
citation: USWDS. Sidenav — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Sidenav — when to consider something else
title: Sidenav — when to consider something else: Existing navigation.
statement: Existing navigation. If your page already has a horizontal and vertical navigation bar, consider ways to simplify your navigation system.
citation: USWDS. Sidenav — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Sidenav — when to use: To display a navigational hierarchy with one to three levels.
statement: To display a navigational hierarchy with one to three levels. - To display the “sub-navigation” within a section of the website.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Site Alert — accessibility: Don’t visually hide alert messages and then make them visible when they are needed.
statement: Don’t visually hide alert messages and then make them visible when they are needed. Users of older assistive technologies may still be able to perceive hidden alert messages. Fully remove alert messages when they’re not needed.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Site Alert — accessibility: Include a descriptive ARIA label.
statement: Include a descriptive ARIA label. Add an aria-label or aria-labelledby attribute to the .usa-site-alert element to ensure that your site alert appears in the landmarks menu. A well-written label can help assistive technology users easily find and understand the top-level information of your site alert.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Site Alert — accessibility: Add an ARIA role to dynamically-updated site alerts.
statement: Add an ARIA role to dynamically-updated site alerts. For important, time-sensitive site alerts that will receive new content mid-session, for example if your site pushes out an updated emergency alert, add an ARIA role attribute that will notify users of changes. To do this, choose the appropriate role from the ARIA roles table and add it to the .usa-site-alert element.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Site Alert — usability: Place prominently.
statement: Place prominently. Use a full-width site alert positioned near the top of the page so it's one of the first things users see.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Site Alert — usability: Avoid stacking multiple site alerts.
statement: Avoid stacking multiple site alerts. If you need to convey more than one message, provide a list of links within a single site alert instead of multiple, stacked alerts.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Site Alert — usability: Avoid overwhelming use of color.
statement: Avoid overwhelming use of color. It may be tempting to make heavy use of bright red or orange to draw attention to an emergency-related site alert. However, these colors can produce strong negative emotional reactions such as fear or panic. Positioning the banner at the top of the screen provides enough weight that such strong colors may not be necessary.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Site Alert — when to consider something else
title: Site Alert — when to consider something else: Responding to user actions.
statement: Responding to user actions. Use the alert component for page-level validation messages (like error messages on a form) or to inform a user that a task was completed successfully.
citation: USWDS. Site Alert — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Site Alert — when to consider something else
title: Site Alert — when to consider something else: Validating form input.
statement: Validating form input. On most forms, especially longer forms, validation messages should appear inline with error messages at the top of the form.
citation: USWDS. Site Alert — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Site Alert — when to use: Critical system notifications.
statement: Critical system notifications. Use a site alert to deliver a static system status update, such as notices about unavailable services or content. Site alerts should appear by default and not in response to an action.
citation: USWDS. Site Alert — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Site Alert — when to use: Messages that should be displayed on every page.
statement: Messages that should be displayed on every page. A site alert makes critical information obvious and findable on every page.
citation: USWDS. Site Alert — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — accessibility: Use semantic heading levels.
statement: Use semantic heading levels. Though our default code uses an , use the correct heading level in your own implementation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — accessibility: Use visually hidden text on labels.
statement: Use visually hidden text on labels. Use visually hidden text make the completion status of each step explicit.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — accessibility: Indicate the current step.
statement: Indicate the current step. When using labeled segments, use aria-current="true" on the list item representing the current step.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — accessibility: Hide unlabeled segments.
statement: Hide unlabeled segments. There is no content inside the segments when labels aren't used, so it is safe to add aria-hidden="true" to the element with the class name usa-step-indicatorsegments.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: Use counters to reinforce step progression.
statement: Use counters to reinforce step progression. The counter pattern (step numbers in a circle) attracts more attention to the indicator bar, but more strongly communicates step-by-step progression. Use counters when you want to reinforce step progression. Omit them if testing proves that this reinforcement is unnecessary for your audience.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: Omit labels with verbose content.
statement: Omit labels with verbose content. Aim for clear and crisp labels. Omit labels to save space or if the step names are too long to comfortably fit in the step indicator.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: Use the centered variant with centered content and headings.
statement: Use the centered variant with centered content and headings. The centered variant is designed to complement centered content and headings. If you have left-aligned content and headings, use the default alignment.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: Center the heading with utilities.
statement: Center the heading with utilities. Use the flex-justify-center utility on usa-step-indicatorheader to center the heading.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: Centered counters need narrower gaps and a thinner segment.
statement: Centered counters need narrower gaps and a thinner segment. If you use a centered variant with counters, you should use a narrower gap (2px is a good starting point) to increase the continuity between segments. A narrower counter gap (again, 2px is a good starting point) can also improve legibility. Centered counters can also benefit from a thinner segment, as the centered variant focusses emphasis on the counter instead of the segment.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: Pending text should use gray.
statement: Pending text should use gray. Pending text should use the gray family that complements the background and the pending segment colors. Use warm grays with warm backgrounds and segments, and cool grays with cool backgrounds and segments.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: Pending segments can use gray or complete family.
statement: Pending segments can use gray or complete family. Pending segments can use gray, just as with pending text, but they can also use a light grade of the complete color family.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: The current color can be a contrast color.
statement: The current color can be a contrast color. The current color can be in the same family as the complete color or it can be a contrast color that distinguishes itself from the complete color.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: Thicker segments use wider counter gaps.
statement: Thicker segments use wider counter gaps. It can be distracting to use a thick segment with a narrow counter gap. Use a gap of at least 0.5 units on a 1 unit segment.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — implementation: Avoid wide counter gaps.
statement: Avoid wide counter gaps. Counter gaps can improve legibility of the counters, but wide counter gaps hurt the overall continuity between the counters and the segments.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — usability: Indicate where a user is in the process.
statement: Indicate where a user is in the process. Use a color and text treatment for the current step segment that is distinct from both the completed and pending step segments. The current segment should be the most visually prominent segment in the step indicator. Pending segments should be the least visually prominent of the segments, but should still maintain accessible contrast and not appear disabled.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — usability: Use short or single-word labels.
statement: Use short or single-word labels. If labelling the step indicators, stick to very short words.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — usability: Provide navigation separately.
statement: Provide navigation separately. Use navigation like a button group to step forward and backward through a form.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — usability: Place a heading directly below the step indicator.
statement: Place a heading directly below the step indicator. Each step needs an explicit heading. The step indicator segments (even with labels and counters) are not sufficient as a heading for a page or screen.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — usability: Display step and total left of the heading.
statement: Display step and total left of the heading. Using text like "[step] of [total]" next to the heading reinforces the number of total steps and helps users keep track of their location in the overall process.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Step Indicator — when to consider something else
title: Step Indicator — when to consider something else: Long forms with conditional logic.
statement: Long forms with conditional logic. Consider another approach if the number of steps might change due to user input.
citation: USWDS. Step Indicator — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Step Indicator — when to consider something else
title: Step Indicator — when to consider something else: Nonlinear progression.
statement: Nonlinear progression. The step indicator isn't appropriate for nonlinear forms or interactions that might be completed in any order.
citation: USWDS. Step Indicator — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Step Indicator — when to consider something else
title: Step Indicator — when to consider something else: Very short forms.
statement: Very short forms. Don’t use a step indicator for short forms without chapters or sections. If a form or process has fewer than three sections, don't use a step indicator.
citation: USWDS. Step Indicator — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — when to use: Multiple steps and screens.
statement: Multiple steps and screens. Use the step indicator when the user is working through a form or process that will span several different pages that can be organized into three or more high-level steps or chapters. This helps users understand the progression of long forms and reduces uncertainty as they complete each screen.
citation: USWDS. Step Indicator — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Step Indicator — when to use: Linear progression.
statement: Linear progression. The step indicator is designed to complement standard back/next navigation in a linear sequence, not to be navigation of its own.
citation: USWDS. Step Indicator — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Summary Box — accessibility: Write for your audience.
statement: Write for your audience. The summary box is meant to make it easier to understand page content. Don't leave readers without access to critical information. Check your writing level to ensure it’s easy to read. Search for "readability level tool" to find tools that assess reading level.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Summary Box — usability: Select, split, and sequence to prioritize critical information.
statement: Select, split, and sequence to prioritize critical information. First, select the most important information from the page. Then, split up the information into logical parts. Finally, sequence the parts in an order that makes sense to the reader.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Summary Box — usability: Link to more information.
statement: Link to more information. We suggest linking to further reading on the same page using an anchor link. To do this without confusing your readers, do your best to explain where the link will take them in the hyperlinked text and reiterate it with the subsequent heading.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Summary Box — usability: Use smooth scrolling.
statement: Use smooth scrolling. Show the reader that they haven’t left the page with smooth scrolling. If you opt for smooth scrolling, ensure the focus state is transferred appropriately.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Summary Box — usability: Give the user a way to get back.
statement: Give the user a way to get back. Provide a “back to top” link or sticky internal navigation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Summary Box — when to consider something else
title: Summary Box — when to consider something else: Internal page navigation.
statement: Internal page navigation. Don't use a summary box as a table of contents. If you’re listing headings for internal page navigation, use a simple unordered list of jump links or side navigation.
citation: USWDS. Summary Box — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Summary Box — when to consider something else
title: Summary Box — when to consider something else: Your page is short.
statement: Your page is short. The summary box gives users quick access to the most important information on a long page. If your page isn’t that long, a recap may feel redundant.
citation: USWDS. Summary Box — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Summary Box — when to consider something else
title: Summary Box — when to consider something else: Your list needs more detail.
statement: Your list needs more detail. Summary boxes should be short. Use a process list, graphic list, or icon list in the body of the article when:
citation: USWDS. Summary Box — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Summary Box — when to consider something else
title: Summary Box — when to consider something else: Alerts or callouts.
statement: Alerts or callouts. you’re highlighting something new, rather than surfacing details from further down the page, use the alert component, such as the informative status alert.
citation: USWDS. Summary Box — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Summary Box — when to use: Summarize dense content.
statement: Summarize dense content. If your page contains a lot of information, use the summary box to call out 3-5 key details that readers shouldn't miss.
citation: USWDS. Summary Box — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Summary Box — when to use: Highlight a short, actionable list.
statement: Highlight a short, actionable list. If the page content describes a few steps or a checklist of items to remember, collect them in a summary box. Use five bullet points or less.
citation: USWDS. Summary Box — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — accessibility: Simple tables can have up to two rows of headers.
statement: Simple tables can have up to two rows of headers. Each header cell should have scope="col" or scope="row".

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — accessibility: Complex tables have more than two levels of headers.
statement: Complex tables have more than two levels of headers. Each header should have a unique id and each data cell should have a headers attribute with each related header cell’s id listed.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — accessibility: Add title and attribution in a caption.
statement: Add title and attribution in a caption. When adding a title, attribution, or a last-updated date to a table, include it in the tag inside of the element.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — accessibility: Add an aria-live region to the page when enabling row sorting.
statement: Add an aria-live region to the page when enabling row sorting. An aria-live region immediately following the element automatically announces when the sort state changes for visitors using screen readers, but it must be added to the HTML document before load:

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — accessibility: Don’t add aria-label attributes to sortable column headers.
statement: Don’t add aria-label attributes to sortable column headers. Enabling row sorting automatically adds aria-label attributes to the sortable column headers and their toggle sort buttons via JavaScript. These labels are updated to reflect each column’s current sort state (ascending, descending, or unsorted) whenever sort changes.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — accessibility: Scrollable tables need to be focusable.
statement: Scrollable tables need to be focusable. When you use the .usa-table-container--scrollable variant with a table, you must add the tabindex="0" attribute to the scrollable element. This attribute assures that users navigating with a keyboard are able to select and scroll the table. tabindex="0" enables focus on elements that do not get focus by default. This attribute does not change the tab order. It places the element in the logical navigation flow.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — implementation: Enable row sorting on columns with sortable data.
statement: Enable row sorting on columns with sortable data. To activate row sorting, add the data-sortable attribute to the table header element ( ) of any column with sortable data, and insert an element with the aria-live="polite" attribute and the class .usa-tableannouncement-region immediately following the table.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — implementation: Set a default sort column and direction.
statement: Set a default sort column and direction. To sort a table’s rows by a specific sortable column on load, add the attribute aria-sort equal to a sort direction, such as “ascending” or “descending,” to that column header as in the following example:

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — implementation: Provide raw values for cells with formatted number content.
statement: Provide raw values for cells with formatted number content. If you have formatted your cell content for display (such as using percent, currency, or comma formatting) or if your cell content is non-numeric but should be sorted in a numeric order (such as months, days of the week, or dates), provide a numeric-sortable value in a data-sort-value attribute on each table cell. Examples follow:

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Keep it simple.
statement: Keep it simple. Tables are great at displaying data and complex information. Minimal visual styling helps surface this information more easily.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Always use a header row.
statement: Always use a header row. Use plain language and short labels to define the type of information that can be found in each column or row. For more complex table structures, review the WCAG accessibility recommendations for tables.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Predictably format columns.
statement: Predictably format columns. Take care not to vary units or formatting within the same column. Instead, normalize values so they can be easily compared. For example, if most of the rows in a table show a count in days, don’t have some rows that count by weeks.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Right-align numerical data.
statement: Right-align numerical data. Align numbers that represent a sum to the right using the text alignment utilities on the table cells.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Use a monospace font for numerical data.
statement: Use a monospace font for numerical data. For even better readability of dense, numerical data, consider formatting numbers that convey amounts, such as percentages, currency, or tallies, in a monospace font. (There’s no need to apply monospace formatting or alignment to phone numbers, zip codes, dates, or other number content that can’t be totaled.)

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Attribute table data in a caption.
statement: Attribute table data in a caption. If your table includes information from a specific source or contains frequently updated content, provide the source and/or last updated date. This clarification is especially useful if your table summarizes data from a more extensive source.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Consider a small-screen experience.
statement: Consider a small-screen experience. On mobile devices and other small screens, numerical data across many columns can be easier to understand if the table scrolls horizontally. Directory lists are more readable if the rows display in a stacked layout. For tables with more than two columns, make sure you choose either a scrollable or a stacked variant.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Minimize the number of columns.
statement: Minimize the number of columns. It’s easier for users to read down a long list of rows than it is to read across a long list of columns. Eliminate columns when possible, or consider swapping the columns and rows to improve scannability.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Enable sort where useful.
statement: Enable sort where useful. Add row sorting to individual columns of long tables where the data can be logically ordered either alphabetically or numerically.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Don’t use row sorting with merged cells.
statement: Don’t use row sorting with merged cells. Sorting won’t work properly if your table contains colspan or rowspan attributes on the cells.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — usability: Don’t use row sorting with the mobile stacked variants.
statement: Don’t use row sorting with the mobile stacked variants. Sorting won’t work properly with these variants because the column headers at the top of the table don’t appear at narrow widths and are instead moved into the cell content in each row.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Table — when to consider something else
title: Table — when to consider something else: Non-tabular data.
statement: Non-tabular data. Depending on the type of content, consider using other presentation formats, such as definition lists or hierarchical lists.
citation: USWDS. Table — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Table — when to consider something else
title: Table — when to consider something else: Robust data visualization.
statement: Robust data visualization. If you need to display more complex relationships or data visualizations, consider a bar graph, infographic, or other type of chart.
citation: USWDS. Table — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Table — when to consider something else
title: Table — when to consider something else: Dashboards and other layouts.
statement: Dashboards and other layouts. Don’t use tables in place of a layout grid. Table content should follow a consistent structure using headers and logical columns and rows.
citation: USWDS. Table — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Table — when to consider something else
title: Table — when to consider something else: Long-form content.
statement: Long-form content. Table cell content should be brief and scannable. If you find yourself drafting multiple bullet points or paragraphs within a single table cell, the content is likely better off under conventional page headers or in an accordion.
citation: USWDS. Table — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Table — when to consider something else
title: Table — when to consider something else: Groups of items with different structures.
statement: Groups of items with different structures. Consider a list or cards for content items that don’t follow a consistent pattern.
citation: USWDS. Table — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — when to use: Displaying tabular data.
statement: Displaying tabular data. When you need to display tabular information, such as statistical data.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Table — when to use: Displaying directories.
statement: Displaying directories. When listing locations or resources that have similarly structured content for many items.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tag — accessibility: Use ARIA live regions to highlight dynamically loaded content.
statement: Use ARIA live regions to highlight dynamically loaded content. When tags are used to call out new content that is dynamically loaded onto a page, be sure to use ARIA live regions to alert screen readers of the change.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tag — usability: Users frequently confuse tags as buttons.
statement: Users frequently confuse tags as buttons. Always conduct usability testing to make sure your particular implementation is not causing frustration.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tag — usability: If your tags aren’t interactive, disable hover, focus, and active styles.
statement: If your tags aren’t interactive, disable hover, focus, and active styles. - Don’t mix interactive and static tags. Once you establish a pattern for how tags behave on your site, users will expect that behavior every time.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tag — usability: Don’t overdo it.
statement: Don’t overdo it. If everything on a page is called out as important, nothing commands unique attention.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Tag — when to consider something else
title: Tag — when to consider something else: Confusion with buttons.
statement: Confusion with buttons. Avoid tags if they might appear in the same area of the page as buttons.
citation: USWDS. Tag — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Tag — when to consider something else
title: Tag — when to consider something else: New or updated content.
statement: New or updated content. To call attention to new or updated content, consider changing the background color of the object itself or experiment with changing the font weight.
citation: USWDS. Tag — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Tag — when to consider something else
title: Tag — when to consider something else: When users already expect content to be updated frequently.
statement: When users already expect content to be updated frequently. For example, on a site dedicated to breaking news. In this case placing the new content at the top may be enough.
citation: USWDS. Tag — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tag — when to use: To draw attention to new, important content.
statement: To draw attention to new, important content. Tags can focus attention on important content on that might otherwise be missed.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tag — when to use: To filter results with one or more tags.
statement: To filter results with one or more tags. - To indicate the number of new or unread items within a container. For example, to indicate the number of unread emails within a person’s inbox.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — accessibility: Avoid placeholder text.
statement: Avoid placeholder text. Most browsers’ default rendering of placeholder text does not provide a high enough contrast ratio.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — accessibility: Avoid splitting numbers.
statement: Avoid splitting numbers. Avoid breaking numbers with distinct sections (such as phone numbers, Social Security Numbers, or credit card numbers) into separate input fields. For example, use one input for phone number, not three (one for area code, one for local code, and one for number). Each field needs to be labeled for a screen reader and the labels for fields broken into segments are often not meaningful.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — accessibility: Choose disabled or read-only behavior deliberately.
statement: Choose disabled or read-only behavior deliberately. A native disabled input cannot be edited or reached with the Tab key, and its value is not submitted with the form. A readonly text input remains focusable and its value is submitted. Use read-only behavior when users need to review or copy a value.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — accessibility: Do not rely on aria-disabled alone.
statement: Do not rely on aria-disabled alone. aria-disabled="true" communicates that a text input is unavailable and applies disabled styles. It does not prevent editing. Your application must enforce the intended behavior and explain why the field is unavailable.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — usability: Use fields appropriate to the length of the input.
statement: Use fields appropriate to the length of the input. The length of the text input provides a hint to users as to how much text to write. Do not require users to write paragraphs of text into a single-line input box; use a text area instead.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — usability: Consider the mobile context.
statement: Consider the mobile context. Text inputs are among the easiest type of input for desktop users but are more difficult for mobile users.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — usability: Wait to validate.
statement: Wait to validate. Only show error validation messages or stylings after a user has interacted with a particular field.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — usability: Avoid placeholder text.
statement: Avoid placeholder text. Avoid using placeholder text that appears within a text field before a user starts typing. If placeholder text is no longer visible after a user clicks into the field, users will no longer have that text available when they need to review their entries. (People who have cognitive or visual disabilities have additional problems with placeholder text.)

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Text Input — when to consider something else
title: Text Input — when to consider something else: Predetermined input options.
statement: Predetermined input options. When users are choosing from a specific set of options.
citation: USWDS. Text Input — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — when to use: Unpredictable or freeform responses.
statement: Unpredictable or freeform responses. If you can’t reasonably predict a user’s answer to a prompt and there might be wide variability in users’ answers.
citation: USWDS. Text Input — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — when to use: Input simplicity.
statement: Input simplicity. When using another type of input will make answering more difficult. For example, birthdays and other known dates are easier to type in than they are to select from a date picker.
citation: USWDS. Text Input — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Text Input — when to use: Pasted content.
statement: Pasted content. When users want to be able to paste in a response.
citation: USWDS. Text Input — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — accessibility: Customize form controls accessibly.
statement: Customize form controls accessibly. If you customize this component, ensure that it continues to meet the accessibility requirements that apply to all form controls.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — accessibility: Always use a label.
statement: Always use a label. Make sure your select element has a label. Don’t replace it with the default menu option (for example, removing the “State” label and just having the menu read “Select a state” by default).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — accessibility: Avoid auto-submission.
statement: Avoid auto-submission. Don’t use JavaScript to automatically submit the form (or do anything else) when an option is selected. Auto-submission disrupts screen readers because they select each option as they read them.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — implementation: Properties.
statement: Properties. The following properties modify component functionality. These properties can be set or adjusted at any time before or after initialization in order to have an effect.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — implementation: Initialization properties.
statement: Initialization properties. The following properties update the component during initialization. These properties must be set before the component is initialized in order to have an effect.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — implementation: Procedures.
statement: Procedures. The following static procedures update the component after initialization. These are in addition to the primary methods referenced in the JS customization documentation.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — usability: Make sure to test.
statement: Make sure to test. Test select menus thoroughly with members of your target audience. Several usability experts suggest they should be the “UI of last resort.” Many users find them confusing and difficult to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — usability: Avoid dependent options.
statement: Avoid dependent options. Avoid making options in one select menu change based on the input to another. Users often don’t understand how choosing an item in one impacts another

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — usability: Use a good default.
statement: Use a good default. When most users will (or should) pick a particular option, make it the default: Default .

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — usability: Avoid auto-submission.
statement: Avoid auto-submission. Don’t use JavaScript to automatically submit the form (or do anything else) when an option is selected. Offer a “submit” button at the end of the form instead. Users often change their choices multiple times. Auto-submission is also less accessible.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Time Picker — when to consider something else
title: Time Picker — when to consider something else: Exact time.
statement: Exact time. Plain text input is more appropriate for historical exact times, like time of birth.
citation: USWDS. Time Picker — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Time Picker — when to use: Scheduling.
statement: Scheduling. Use the time picker to schedule a time from common, consistent increments, such as planning a meeting time in 30-minute blocks.
citation: USWDS. Time Picker — when to use.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — accessibility: Use as title attribute.
statement: Use as title attribute. Tooltips are progressive enhancements for the title attribute, and will display as the title attribute if the component doesn’t initialize.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — accessibility: Keyboard accessibility.
statement: Keyboard accessibility. Tooltips make title attributes keyboard accessible.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — implementation: Tooltip — implementation
statement: - Any element with the class name usa-tooltip and a title attribute will become a tooltip. - Place tooltips on elements with as few child elements as possible. - Elements or text that show a tooltip when hovered or focused will not wrap onto a new line and will get tabindex="0" for keyboard interaction. - By default, tooltips appear on the top of their related element. - Use the data-position attribute to indicate the tooltip's position in relation to the related element: - data-position="top": On top, horizontally centered. If the data-position attribute is omitted, the tooltip will appear on top by default. - data-position="bottom": Below, horizontally centered - data-position="right": To the right, vertically centered - data-position="left": To the left, vertically centered - Tooltips are protected from viewport clipping. If clipping is detected, the tooltip is positioned on the opposite side as data-position attribute indicates. If the tooltip is still clipped, it is positioned on top of the element, with its width constrained to the width its related element. Only then does the tooltip wrap to multiple lines. - JavaScript generated most of the tooltip’s markup. Apply utility classes to any tooltip’s wrapping element, by including them inside a data-classes attribute, separated by spaces.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — usability: Make tooltips discoverable.
statement: Make tooltips discoverable. A hidden tooltip is unusable. Use tooltips only on elements that appear interactive, like buttons or links.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — usability: Avoid collisions.
statement: Avoid collisions. Be careful not introduce conflicting hover or focus events.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — usability: Use consistently.
statement: Use consistently. If using tooltips in one context, use in all similar contexts.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — usability: Don’t block content.
statement: Don’t block content. Use the data-position attribute to prevent the tooltip from covering other page elements.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Tooltip — when to consider something else
title: Tooltip — when to consider something else: Critical information.
statement: Critical information. Don’t hide information necessary for completing a task behind an tooltip interaction.
citation: USWDS. Tooltip — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Tooltip — when to consider something else
title: Tooltip — when to consider something else: Lengthy descriptions.
statement: Lengthy descriptions. Tooltips are microcopy, and should be brief. Don't use a tooltip if you need a lot of text.
citation: USWDS. Tooltip — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Tooltip — when to consider something else
title: Tooltip — when to consider something else: Redundant content.
statement: Redundant content. Don’t use a tooltip when its content is repetitive or if usability is obvious.
citation: USWDS. Tooltip — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Tooltip — when to consider something else
title: Tooltip — when to consider something else: Sufficient space.
statement: Sufficient space. If content can fit outside a tooltip, don't use a tooltip.
citation: USWDS. Tooltip — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — when to use: Helpful, non-critical information.
statement: Helpful, non-critical information. Use tooltips to strengthen an existing message.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — when to use: Enhance confidence.
statement: Enhance confidence. Use tooltips to increase certainty about an interaction.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — when to use: Brief descriptions.
statement: Brief descriptions. Tooltips perform best with succinct helper text.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Tooltip — when to use: Lack of space.
statement: Lack of space. Tooltips are useful as a last resort for space-constrained UI. Explore other options for keeping content visible without a tooltip.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Validation — implementation: Validate on the server side as well.
statement: Validate on the server side as well. The validation component is intended primarily for usability, not as a robust security solution, since all the validation logic occurs on the client side. The validation should be "mirrored" on the server-side for security purposes.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Validation — implementation: Connect the input element to your validation checklist.
statement: Connect the input element to your validation checklist. Set the value of your input's data-validation-element to the id of its related .usa-checklist. For example, if the .usa-checklist element has an id of validate-code, use data-validation-element="validate-code".

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Validation — implementation: Customize the validation attributes.
statement: Customize the validation attributes. For each type of validation you'd like to provide feedback on:

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Validation — when to use: Validation — when to use
statement: Provide helpful validation feedback. Use the validation component to give immediate feedback on which validation requirements have been successfully met, and which are not completed yet.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language — accessibility: Code header areas in the accordion as buttons.
statement: Code header areas in the accordion as buttons. Using a assures accordions are usable with both screen readers and keyboards.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language — accessibility: Use aria-expanded on buttons to express an accordion’s default state.
statement: Use aria-expanded on buttons to express an accordion’s default state. Buttons should state if they are expanded by default with aria-expanded="true". The aria-expanded="false" attribute will be added to other buttons when the accordion is initialized by the JavaScript.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language — accessibility: Use unique ids.
statement: Use unique ids. Each button has a unique name, aria-controls="id", that associates the control with the appropriate region by referencing the controlled element’s id.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language — accessibility: Accordions use javascript to set the hidden values of their content areas.
statement: Accordions use javascript to set the hidden values of their content areas. Each content area will have its hidden attribute set by the component, depending on its corresponding button’s aria-expanded attribute. To ensure your content is accessible in the event that the JavaScript does not load or is disabled, you should not manually set hidden on any of your content areas.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language — implementation: Multiselectable accordion groups.
statement: Multiselectable accordion groups. Add the aria-multiselectable="true" attribute to any usa-accordion to create a multiselectable accordion group.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language — implementation: Default an accordion button to open.
statement: Default an accordion button to open. Add the aria-expanded="true" attribute to any usa-accordionbutton to have that section open by default at page load.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language — usability: Make the entire header selectable.
statement: Make the entire header selectable. Allow users to click anywhere in the header area to expand or collapse the content; a larger target is easier to manipulate.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language — usability: Give interactive elements enough space.
statement: Give interactive elements enough space. Make sure interactive elements within the collapsible region are far enough from the headers that users don’t accidentally trigger a collapse. (The exact distance depends on the device.)

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Language — when to consider something else
title: Language — when to consider something else: If users need to see most or all of the information on a page.
statement: If users need to see most or all of the information on a page. Use well-formatted text instead.
citation: USWDS. Language — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
subcategory: Language — when to consider something else
title: Language — when to consider something else: If there is not enough content to warrant condensing.
statement: If there is not enough content to warrant condensing. Accordions increase cognitive load and interaction cost because users have to make decisions about what headers to click on.
citation: USWDS. Language — when to consider something else.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language — when to use: If users will only need a few specific pieces of content within a page.
statement: If users will only need a few specific pieces of content within a page. - If you have only a small space to display a lot of content.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language: What problem does this solve?
statement: We envision empowered agency digital teams who share solutions and use effective human-centered design practices. {:.margin-top-4}

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language: Websites with two languages
statement: USWDS is the design system for the federal government. We make it easier to build accessible, mobile-friendly government websites. {:.margin-top-2}

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Language: What's the solution?
statement: Place a button in the upper right of the navigation to allow the user to toggle between the two languages

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Start early.
statement: Start early. Early in the project, spend time with current and prospective users to better understand their perspective and the context of the problem.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Use a range of methods.
statement: Use a range of methods. Use a range of qualitative and quantitative research methods (such as 18F Methods) to determine people’s goals, needs, and behaviors.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Use prototypes.
statement: Use prototypes. Use prototypes to test your assumptions and solutions with real people, in the field if possible.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Share your findings.
statement: Share your findings. Document and share your research findings with team members, managers, and the public whenever practical.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Test regularly.
statement: Test regularly. As the product is being built, regularly test it with potential or current users to ensure it meets people’s needs.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Identify yourself.
statement: Identify yourself. Clearly identify your site as a federal government site.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Build with modern best practices.
statement: Build with modern best practices. Review the guidance outlined in the Digital Services Playbook.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Review your content.
statement: Review your content. Review your content at least twice a year to assure information is correct and non-redundant.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Use the proper government domain.
statement: Use the proper government domain. Use a .gov top-level domain and https with up-to-date certificates.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Add the USWDS banner component.
statement: Add the USWDS banner component. This component shows your site is an official government website and explains the benefits of secure connections.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Identify link rot.
statement: Identify link rot. Find and fix broken links on your website.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Keep communications simple.
statement: Keep communications simple. Ensure content is easy, personal, and timely.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Write for the web.
statement: Write for the web. Expect users to skim and scan.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Properly manage data and records.
statement: Properly manage data and records. Reach out to your agency’s records officer and privacy official. Consult with them to make sure you're properly managing data and records (review play 11, Manage security and privacy through reusable processes, in the Digital Services Playbook).

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Understand expectations.
statement: Understand expectations. Understand what your audience expects of your service, and validate the success of your service with real users.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Publish open code and data.
statement: Publish open code and data. When appropriate, publish source code and datasets of projects or components online.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Work in the open.
statement: Work in the open. When appropriate, share your development process and progress publicly.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Humanize accessibility.
statement: Humanize accessibility. Seek out examples of the real-life impact of accessible products and services. Try to make accessibility less abstract and more personal.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Use agency resources.
statement: Use agency resources. Reach out to your agency's accessibility team, and build a relationship with them.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Learn about assistive technology.
statement: Learn about assistive technology. Visit the Web Accessibility Initiative website to get familiar with the basic ways people use assistive technology and how people with disabilities use the web.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Follow existing standards.
statement: Follow existing standards. Conform to the Revised 508 Standards and W3C WCAG 2.1.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Work from existing resources.
statement: Work from existing resources. Consult Section508.gov, Accessibility for Teams, and the 18F Accessibility Guide.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Develop accessible code.
statement: Develop accessible code. Ensure front-end code is written accessibly and conducts manual and automated testing.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Write accessible content.
statement: Write accessible content. Ensure content is written in plain language and headings, images, and links are accurately labeled.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Build accessible designs.
statement: Build accessible designs. Ensure designs are accessible, pages are laid out in a logical order, and content meets color-contrast requirements.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Test broadly.
statement: Test broadly. Test with a broad range of users and abilities throughout the design and development process, including manual accessibility testing using the Trusted Tester and ICT Testing Baseline.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Be responsive.
statement: Be responsive. Fix accessibility issues when you discover them.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Contract for accessibility.
statement: Contract for accessibility. Use the Accessibility Requirements Tool (ART) to incorporate accessibility requirements into your contracts.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Identify as a government site.
statement: Identify as a government site. Clearly and consistently identify as a government site on every page.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Use a style guide.
statement: Use a style guide. Use a simple and flexible style guide for content and style throughout a product or service. Find out if existing guides already exist in your agency before developing something new.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Connect related services with a similar style.
statement: Connect related services with a similar style. Use the style guide consistently for related digital services.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Support a wide range of devices and platforms.
statement: Support a wide range of devices and platforms. Support a wide range of devices for a mobile-friendly experience.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Test on real devices.
statement: Test on real devices. Test your site on the actual mobile devices as often as possible.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Move or remove content with care.
statement: Move or remove content with care. Provide proper notice and forwarding when content is moved or removed.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Clarify multi-step processes.
statement: Clarify multi-step processes. Give users clear information about where they are in each step of a process.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Support multi-session processes.
statement: Support multi-session processes. Provide users with a way to exit and return later to complete a process.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Support re-use of saved data.
statement: Support re-use of saved data. Assure that repeat website visitors who have logged in can auto-populate forms with saved information.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Find a community.
statement: Find a community. Participate in cross-government communities of practice.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Actively collect issues.
statement: Actively collect issues. Offer users a mechanism to report bugs and issues, and be responsive to these reports.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Collect direct feedback.
statement: Collect direct feedback. Actively collect, review, and address feedback about your product or service through methods like surveys or customer emails.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Analyze analytics data.
statement: Analyze analytics data. Implement both the government-wide Digital Analytics Program (DAP) and agency-specific analytics services, and analyze the data.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Analyze search results.
statement: Analyze search results. Include a search function on your site (through Search.gov or another tool), and analyze the search data.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Analyze social media data.
statement: Analyze social media data. If you use social media platforms, analyze the data from these platforms.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Publish metrics.
statement: Publish metrics. Publish metrics internally and externally.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Coordinate large projects with service design.
statement: Coordinate large projects with service design. Conduct a service design analysis when designing, coordinating, or consolidating large sites or services.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Involve the team in research.
statement: Involve the team in research. Involve all members of a project team in user interviews and research activities to hear directly from real users.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Use direct observation.
statement: Use direct observation. Use direct observation in your research whenever possible to understand the context of a user's actions.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Keep testing.
statement: Keep testing. Test and re-test with real users.

author: U.S. General Services Administration
title: Overview: Share back.
statement: Share back. Contribute feedback and share solutions back to the internal and open source projects you use.
